speechtext:
In accordance with standing order 25, Mr. Speaker, Beauchesne, second edition, I should like to move, seconded by the hon. member for Saint John-Albert (Mr. Hazen):
That Bill No. 301, an act for the relief of Aldoria Rodier ddt St. Martin, referred to in the third report of the standing committee on private bills, presented to this house this day, be referred back to the standing committee for further consideration and report.
This is a bill for divorce which was brought before the senate committee, where evidence was taken therein in full. After the applicant had presented his ease, counsel for the respondent stated that they had no evidence to adduce in rebuttal of the allegation made by the applicant. The committee of the other house agreed to the divorce and recommended that it be granted. On presentation of the bill a few days ago to the miscellaneous private bills committee of the House of Commons, there appeared the evidence taken in the senate, the recommendations of the senate committee, and, although the counsel for the respondent had stated before that committee that they had no evidence to offer in rebuttal of the evidence of the applicant, a letter from the respondent herself was, I submit, wrongly admitted into evidence by the committee of this house. By virtue of that letter, objecting to certain procedures and certain evidence given, the committee of the House of Commons I believe rejected the bill.
My point is this. A committee of the upper house sitting as a court, having gone into the evidence in detail, having passed upon it, having had witnesses before it who were examined and cross-examined, and counsel for the respondent having stated that there was no defence to offer, I think it was improper and unjust that a letter should be received from the respondent, taken into consideration and
dealt with by the committee of the House of Commons without opportunity of cross-examination, without evidence being given under oath, and in actual repudiation of the findings of the committee of the upper house. The committee of this house saw fit to give a decision contrary to that of the upper house. This is surely a grave miscarriage of justice.
I think any member of this house who has practised in a court of law will realize the great danger there is in accepting evidence by way of letter, after the case has been closed following a full formal hearing, and taking the weight of that evidence into consideration in deciding upon the disposition of any matter previously considered by a court. Any man with legal experience would realize that it is very improper to receive a letter of that kind anywhere, whether it be a committee of inquiry or a court of any kind. I think it is not only a reflection upon the findings of a very able committee of the other place to overrule a considered opinion reached upon evidence properly adduced and subject to examination and cross-examination; it is an aspersion upon the upper house to have a committee of this house take this action in view of the good work being done in the other place in connection with divorce matters. I believe this would be a dangerous precedent for this house to establish, and it would be doing a grave injustice to a citizen of this country who has taken the only legal recourse available.
Therefore I urge the house, though we are practically at the last day of the session, to adopt the motion and give this applicant the right to a proper hearing and a proper disposition of a proper application to these houses of parliament.

maintopic: MANITOBA NATURAL RESOURCES

speechtext:
Prior to 1930 all ungranted or waste lands in the province of Manitoba were vested in the crown in the right of the Dominion of Canada, and were administered by the government of Canada for the purpose of the dominion, subject to certain conditions and stipulations contained in the agreement for the surrender of Rupert's Land by the Hudson's Bay Company to Her Majesty the Queen.
In August 1928 the present Prime Minister of Canada secured the approval of council to an order which provided that, pursuant to an agreement entered into with the representatives of the government of the province of Manitoba, the province would be placed in a position of equality with the other provinces of confederation with respect to the administration and control of its natural resources as from the entrance of the province into confederation in the year 1870.
A commission consisting of three persons was appointed to inquire into and report as 
to what financial readjustments should be made to effect the desire of the province and the dominion that the province be placed in a position of equality with the other provinces of confederation with respect to the administration and control of its natural resources. As a result of the commission's report, the dominion agreed -to 'transfer to the province for administration and control by the province all the unalienated natural resources within the boundaries of the province, subject to any trust existing in respect thereof and without prejudice to any other interest, other than that of the crown, in the same.
The findings of the commission were agreed to by the government of Canada and the government of the province of Manitoba, and were made the subject matter of an act of the parliament of Canada and of the legislature of the province of Manitoba confirming the same. Subsequently the agreement was confirmed by the parliament of the United Kingdom by an act entitled "The British North America Act, 1930", assented to on the 10th day of July of that year and being chapter 26 of the statutes of the United Kingdom for the year 1930.
The agreement provided, inter alia, for the transfer of unalienated public lands in the province of Manitoba from the dominion to the province. Section 2 provides that the province will carry out in accordance with the terms thereof every contract to purchase or lease any crown lands, mines or minerals and every other arrangement whereby any person has become entitled to any interest therein as against the crown, and further agrees not to affect or alter any term of any such contract to purchase, lease or other arrangement by legislation or otherwise except either with the consent of all the parties thereto other than Canada, or in so far as any legislation may apply generally to all similar agreements relating to lands, mines or minerals in the province or to interests therein irrespective of whom the parties thereto may be.
Under this provision the province could by passing a law of general application expropriate every power site in the province of Manitoba. In this respect it would have the same power that is possessed by the original provinces of confederation. For example, the province of Nova Scotia could, by passing an act of the legislature, expropriate every power site in the province of Nova Scotia; or it could by a similar act expropriate any one or more of the power sites in the province. It is doubtful, however, whether Manitoba

Manitoba Natural Resources Act
could, under the provisions of section 2 of the agreement referred to, expropriate one or two of the power sites in the province, as it could be argued that the law would not be of general application, and therefore any rights granted by the dominion prior to the transfer of the resources to the province could not be interfered with other than by consent of the parties to the arrangement other than Canada. If this contention be well founded, the province of Manitoba would not be in a position of equality with the other provinces of confederation, and as that was the intention of the parties when the resources were transferred, the present bill is to remove any doubt as to the power of the province to do that which the original provinces of confederation could do with respect to property and civil rights within their respective jurisdictions.
The effect of the present bill is to put Manitoba in the same position, as, for instance, Ontario, Quebec and Nova Scotia in respect to their natural resources and to confer upon the legislature of Manitoba the power to deal with civil rights in that province. If the bill is passed it does not confer any power on the government of Manitoba, but it does remove any doubt as to the power of the legislature of the province to deal fully with the property and civil rights of the citizens of Manitoba. Whether or not, in the event of the legislature exercising its power, compensation is to be paid to the owners of property expropriated is a matter for the consideration of the legislature of the province and not for the consideration of parliament.

speechtext: There are two questions which I should like to direct to the Minister of Justice. Under the civil service loyalty regulations, what provision is there for an appeal where a person is rejected? Do regulations exist in writing governing security tests?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. L. ILSLEY (Minister of Justice):
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: CIVIL SERVICE
speechtext:
The answer to the first question of which my hon. friend gave me notice is this: There are no civil service loyalty regulations. As was indicated in the statement made to the house on June 22 (Hansard, page 5629) it is the view of the government that "loyalty to the state of employees in positions of trust ;s an essential aspect of the efficient conduct of public administration". The civil service commission has to satisfy itself as to the character and habits of persons appointed by it to government employment. Where the Civil Service Act and regulations are not applicable, the sole responsibility in this regard falls upon the departments themselves. This responsibility as to character and habits includes the suitability of individual employees from the point of view of security.
In the opinion of the government it would not be appropriate to provide for anything in the nature of a tribunal of loyalty. The government, and the civil service commission within the provisions of the law which governs it, must accept responsibility for all aspects of administration, including that of adequate security within the government service.
The second question was: "Do regulations exist in writing government security tests?" The answer to that question is that there are no regulations governing security tests. However, in the discharge of the government's administrative responsibility the attention of departments and agencies is drawn to the importance of security measures, and procedures have been approved for determining the suitability of employees from a security standpoint.
As was indicated in my statement of June 22, in the government's view loyalty is not

Inquiries oj the Ministry
susceptible to any precise series of tests, and the only specific instruction which has been given by the government on this subject is that which I mentioned at that time, namely, the special case of those who are members of or associated with communist and fascist organizations.

Mr. Speaker, I renew my standing invitation to all to come to Peel a't any time during the next- year.
I wish to direct a question to the Secretary of State for External Affairs. In view of the disturbing press reports with respect to starvation conditions in Berlin, and the apparent move of the Soviet to drive out the other powers from that part of Germany, will the minister indicate what official Canadian personnel are in Berlin at the present time, and also what steps are being taken to protect the interests of Canadians, official or otherwise, in that city?
Right Hon. L. S. ST. LAURENT (Secretary of State for External Affairs): Mr. Speaker, the hon. member let me know just before the house convened that he would ask that question. I have asked my officials for the information. I went to my office just a moment ago, but found that it was not yet ready. I understand that a part of it has to be obtained from the Department of National Defence. The hon. member had
Inquiries of the Ministry

told me that he wished do know those who were there who had dependents with them. That information is being obtained, and I shall give it to the hon. member on my supplementary estimates if there is no opportunity ito do it before.
With respect to the food situation, there is very little I can add to what has already been published in the newspapers. Hon. members know that the Secretary of State for Foreign Affairs at Westminster yesterday made a statement about the situation in Berlin. That is in accordance with the information we have. Of course there is a tense situation there- communications have been interfered with- and it is one that is giving us all concern; but I hope it may be relieved. There have been tense situations there before, and they have been adjusted. I know that every possible effort is being made to adjust this one.

DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL REVENUE Taxation division

297. General administration, including authority to create positions and make appointments, within the division, notwithstanding anything contained in the Civil Service Act and the said positions and staff so appointed are hereby wholly excluded from the operation of the said act, $1,813,574.

maintopic: INCOME TAX ACT
speechtext:
This is the administration section of the taxation division, which deals, I take it, mainly
with income tax. I should like to have the minister say something about the organization of this department. As we all know, over the years a great deal of complaint has been made about delays which I think were to some extent inevitable; however, a great deal of discussion has taken place about them. What is being done to obviate the delays which have been so inconvenient to the taxpayer?-sometimes a stronger word than inconvenient would not foe out of place.
Hon. J. J. MoCANN (Minister of National Revenue): I am glad of the opportunity to say something in reference to the taxation division of the Department of National Revenue. This vote has to do with administration. We at head office are responsible for the administration of the Income War Tax Act, the Excess Profits Tax Act, the Dominion Succession Duty Act, the Canada-United States of America Tax Convention Act of 1943, the Canada-United States of America Tax Convention Act of 1944, the United Kingdom income tax agreement of 1946, the Canada-United Kingdom Succession Duty Agreement of 1946, the provincial corporation income tax of the provinces of British Columbia, Alberta, Saskatchewan, Manitoba, New Brunswick, Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island, and the war salaries order in respect to cases which are not already settled.
As the hon. gentleman knows, the head office of the division is here in Ottawa, and we maintain offices from coast to coast-from Vancouver, Victoria and Yukon across the continent to Sydney, Nova Scotia. We have in all twenty-four or twenty-five offices. In these offices we have an administrative staff including the head office staff, of approximately twelve thousand people. The district-offices are distributed as well as possible, having in mind both the convenience of the public and economy in the administration of the offices.
As the hon. gentleman will understand, returns are made to these several district offices, and cases of assessment where there may be difficulties are referred to head office for adjudication. As to the delay in making assessments, which undoubtedly there has been, I think any fair-minded person will say that is entirely excusable, at least to a point, because of the enormous increase in the amount of work that has to be done. During the war years, as a result of increased taxation and the higher level of earnings of the .people generally, the number of returns greatly increased. For 1946 the returns were approximately 3,565,000. The returns for 1947, which came in at the
Supply-National Revenue

end of May, and the corporation returns which came in at the end of June, will number from
3.800.000	to 4,000,000.
As to the backlog of work to be done to catch up with the assessments, that has been contributed to by several factors. During the war years, for instance, we lost a great number of assessors, auditors and accountants because industry competed with the government for the services of these employees. Industry was able to pay more money to people who could do that work than the government at that time was prepared to pay. That situation has been remedied to a certain extent by a readjustment of salaries throughout the division within the past eighteen months, and also because industry finds that now there is not the need there was during the war years for people who have particular qualifications in the matter of auditing and working out their assessments.
I give this example to the hon. gentleman; I think he can readily understand it, as anyone can-and that is no reflection on my hon. friend. Take a man who has been working in our department. It is the easiest thing in the world for him to go to a firm and say, "I saw your assessment. I had something to do with it in the department, and I believe that if I were in your employ I could show you how to save a considerable sum of money in your taxation." Of course they are glad to pick uip that man and pay him perhaps trwice what we are able to pay him according to the regulations. That is quite legitimate; it is good business for him to do that. But things of that kind depleted the staff of the taxation division; and for that reason, together witli the increased number of returns during the war years, a backlog of work has accumulated.
I am happy to say this condition is being remedied to a great extent. As at June 15 our employees numbered approximately 11,568, which is an increase of about 2,500 over the number we had two years ago. Assessments now are being made at the rate of about
350.000	a month, so we feel that before very long that backlog of work will be cleared away.

maintopic: INCOME TAX ACT
speechtext: Would it be convenient at this point for the minister to tell us what the backlog is?

maintopic: INCOME TAX ACT
speechtext:
I can give it in terms of months. We are about eighteen months behind in our assessments. We hope within a year or two, when we get our staff sufficiently well organized and have the people we desire to get and who will be competent to do the work, that within twelve months after the returns are received all the assessments will be

made, and we shall be able to start the next year with the decks clear. I believe that is a worthy and desirable objective, and that it is good business 'to shoot at that target. Judging by the reports made to me privately as to the progress of the work, I have great hopes that we shall be able to attain that objective within the next year or eighteen months.

maintopic: INCOME TAX ACT
speechtext:
I appreciate the enormous task the department has had to perform, but taking the figures the minister has given, if my arithmetic is correct I find it difficult to see how he can expect to clear up the backlog in anything like the time he has mentioned. Let me see if I have correctly apprehended what the minister said. I understood him to say the backlog was approximately eighteen months. Let us take the returns for a year at 3,700,000, which is just in between the figures for the last two years. If my arithmetic is correct, that would mean a backlog of roughly five and a half million returns. The figure the minister gave as to the rate of progress was
350,000	a month, or 4,200,000 a year, which would be an excess of only about 500,000 over an ordinary year's operations. If my figures are right, unless there is some catch in what I have just said, it would seem more like ten years that will be required.

maintopic: INCOME TAX ACT
speechtext: Oh, no.

maintopic: INCOME TAX ACT
speechtext: Then tell me where I am wrong.

maintopic: INCOME TAX ACT
speechtext: The figures I gave the hon. gentleman have to do with the backlog of work, over and above the current work.

maintopic: INCOME TAX ACT
speechtext: When the minister said eighteen months I took it to mean eighteen months measured in the number of income tax returns that come in, at the rate of nearly four million a year.

maintopic: INCOME TAX ACT
speechtext: I dio not know that I can suggest anything further, except to say we hope that at the end of eighteen months to have the backlog cleared up, and will then be in a position to make assessments of the current year's work.

maintopic: INCOME TAX ACT
speechtext: I do not wish to be unduly persistent. However I should like to be clear on this: When the minister says there are arrears of eighteen months, is it correct to say that the arrears of eighteen months amount to 5,000,000 returns?

maintopic: INCOME TAX ACT
speechtext: No, that is not correct.

What does it mean, then?

The arrears of which I have spoken are not current returns for this year, which are due only on the 26th, which is today. Last year an extension was made to May 31. Those returns came in only at that time. I said there were approximately
3.800,000	of those returns as a backlog of work, and we expect to have cleaned it up within the next eighteen months. It may be optimistic to think that that can be done, in view of the increasing number of returns being put in.

maintopic: INCOME TAX ACT

maintopic: INCOME TAX ACT
speechtext:
I wish to refer to a matter which concerns seriously the southeastern part of British Columbia. I refer to the necessity for the establishment of a district office in that part of the country. I know a committee was appointed-I do not know whether it was an interdepartmental committee or not-to inquire into the matter.
I am sure from their point of view they did what they thought was best. It was proposed to establish an office at Kelowna to serve the Okanagan, and rightly so. Here is a huge area of 40,000 square miles, with over 75,000 people. This area had a production which was valued last year at $127,000,000, and it is not served by a district office of the income tax branch.
It is not as though this situation existed on the prairies, where one can take a car and drive a hundred miles in any direction. As a matter of fact we can do business with Vancouver just as conveniently by train or by mail as we can with Kelowna. Therefore the bulk of business from east and west Kootenay is done through the Vancouver office. We have a large mining and smelting industry, a large lumbering industry, and we do considerable farming. These people are anxious to see a district office established in that area so they may have the opportunity for personal contact which we cannot get by writing letters to Vancouver. I would ask the minister to give the matter serious consideration. I represent one of the most productive constituencies in Canada, one which produces immense wealth, and I think some consideration should be given to the establishment of that office. My suggestion is that the city of Nelson would be the most central point from which to serve the area.

Has the collection

I have a copy of a letter received from the director of income tax in Regina. It is dated June 5, 1948, and is headed, "Collections, J. R. B. 2139". It is addressed to Mr. William Nikota, of Hamton, Saskatchewan, and states:

speechtext: We are doing nothing for which we have not the authority. If that has been done without going through the proper channels and the proper legal procedure, it will not be continued. The hon. member will readily understand that if John Jones is in arrears and owes money, after proper notification if he has not complied with it, it may be necessary to issue a garnishee against money coming to him.

through garnishee?

maintopic: INCOME TAX ACT
speechtext:
There are one or two questions I should like to ask in connection with the collection of income tax. I believe that one of the greatest reasons for the reduction in agricultural production, at a time when food is more necessary than it ever was before, is that the farmers as a whole, while they do not resent the payment of income tax and are willing to do their part in that direction, as they must, do resent what they regard
Supply-National Revenue

as snooper tactics in the investigation of income tax. I shall give an example of this sort of thing which causes resentment.
First I should like to find out from the minister what authority there is for any departmental official to say to young people who work during their summer vacations in order to make it possible for them to go on, to collegiate or university, and who by that method would earn about $400, that whatever they earn immediately becomes part of the father's income. Having earned $400 or more, the father is denied the right to include his son and daughter as dependents. This is carrying bureaucratic tyranny to a limit which parliament ought not to countenance. After all, there are members in all parts of the house who were willing to work during their summer vacations in order to earn sufficient to enable them to continue at school. I have some further questions to ask, but I would like the minister to tell me first under what authority such a ruling has been made.
'Mr. McCANN: I have heard a similar criticism from other sources. My personal understanding is that the provision is statutory, and we are only administering the law as we understand it in the statutes.

maintopic: INCOME TAX ACT
speechtext:
Where is the
statutory authority for it? I have not been able to find it. Certainly I do not ask the minister as head of the department to do other than carry out the law, but I should like to know what section authorizes any officials to make a decision which cannot but be detrimental to the opportunity of many young men and women during their vacations to earn something with which to carry on their education. While the minister is having the section looked up I will continue with other questions.

maintopic: INCOME TAX ACT
speechtext: There is no section, so the hon. member had better not wait too long.

maintopic: INCOME TAX ACT
speechtext:
The minister is
ascertaining how this came about, and I am interested in finding out the justification.
The first question I should like to ask has to do with investigations in general of farmers who are required to make income tax returns. I should like to know how many of the staff the minister has just referred to are engaged as investigators in connection with farmers' income tax returns. How many of those investigators are operating in Canada as a whole, and how many in Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta?
The next question I place before the minister is this:	What is the total amount of
income tax collected from farmers in Canada 
as a whole during the current year, and how much of that was payable in the three western provinces? The reason I ask that is that our farmers in the western provinces feel _ that they are being harassed in connection with the collection of income tax to a greater extent than farmers in other provinces. I ask that question to clarify the situation and to see the actual picture.
About nine months ago an investigation took place in Saskatoon. Certain officials of the income tax department were suspended. It was alleged that they had participated in some kind of arrangement with farmers or taxpayers in general whereby the actual amount to be paid by the individual was concealed in whole or in part. Following the investigation, which the minister told the house about last fall, there were some suspensions. Various investigations took place among farmers, and I am led to believe that several admitted that they had had their income tax returns fixed up in a way that was more generous to them than to the income tax department. Have any prosecutions taken place? Are any being proceeded with? Has the matter been dropped, and if so, is that the end of it?
I should like to ask another question in connection with investigations. On one occasion I asked the minister whether searches were being made of safety deposit boxes in banks without consent of the taxpayer. The answer given was that such was not the fact. I believe every person should discharge his responsibility by paying his income tax, but I do not think anyone can justify an investigator going into a bank and having blanket authority to open up safety deposit boxes. That authority should be given by an order of the court; they should not have that authority on the basis of their own initiative, thereby invading the rights of the individual.
I asked the minister if there had been cases where safety deposit boxes had been opened under ex parte orders issued by a court without the knowledge of the taxpayer. I asked that because while the minister answered me in the negative I have had two or three complaints from farmers in Saskatchewan that they have reason to believe that their safety deposit boxes were entered. The minister said that they would not be without the authority of a court order. Are there cases in which court orders have been issued without the knowledge of the taxpayer?
These are matters which I think our people have a right to know. However commendable may be the efforts of the department-and they are-to assure fairness in the making of

Supply-National Revenue
returns, parliament must be equally astute in seeing that the rights of the individual shall not unnecessarily be invaded, or invaded at all outside the law.
I was particularly struck by the answer given by the minister to the hon. member for York-ton with regard to the holding of certain wheat board certificates as security for income tax in arrears. I am glad the minister was able to give the assurance that that was not being done. It would be an interference by a bureaucrat with the rights of an individual, something that should not be countenanced under any circumstances.

maintopic: INCOME TAX ACT
speechtext: As I remember the hon. member's questions, the first had to do with internal inspection. There are 332 inspectors from one end of Canada to the other. I have not the breakdown as to where they are located, but the last figures I had showed that they were fairly well divided among the several provinces. As far as returns or assessments from farmers are concerned, they are not kept in the division under occupational categories. I could not give the percentage of taxation collections made from farmers, any more than I could give them for textile workers or for any other occupation.

maintopic: INCOME TAX ACT
speechtext:
Has that been
stopped? We did get those figures a couple of years ago.

maintopic: INCOME TAX ACT
speechtext:
We have not the information here, but we can get it. It would entail a great deal of work to keep the figures up to date.
My hon. friend referred particularly to a situation in Saskatoon involving a number of employees. I do not intend to name them. After a thorough investigation, both by the officers of the local Saskatoon office and by our office inspectional staff-which is sometimes confused with the inspectional staff which we call the intelligence staff, having to do with matters of evasion-it was found that a number of employees in Saskatoon had been guilty of fraudulent practices and an entire disregard of regulations. They were suspended, and since then some of them have been dismissed. It is not intended to take any legal action against them by way of prosecution.
I regret that such a thing as this should happen, but if you are to run a department efficiently and have honesty among your employees and fair dealing with the public, you cannot condone practices of the kind. I am sure my hon. friend will agree that were he in my position, or some other position of trust, or in business for himself, and found
that some of his employees were dishonest and would not obey the regulations, he would not continue to employ them.

maintopic: INCOME TAX ACT
speechtext: Quite a number of farmers participated in this fraud to the detriment of the department, 'by falsifying returns. What happened to them?

maintopic: INCOME TAX ACT
speechtext: Those cases were dealt with like any other taxpayer's and if there were penalties applicable they were put into effect. If it was within the province of the division to impose those penalties they were applied.

maintopic: INCOME TAX ACT
speechtext: Were they applied at all?

maintopic: INCOME TAX ACT
speechtext: I am told they were; and if prosecutions were called for, they were undertaken or will be undertaken.

maintopic: INCOME TAX ACT
speechtext: How many taxpayers were involved in this fraud?

maintopic: INCOME TAX ACT
speechtext: I cannot give the details.

maintopic: INCOME TAX ACT
speechtext:
Would not the
minister's official know? I understand that it runs to about fifty.

maintopic: INCOME TAX ACT
speechtext: I do not know.

maintopic: INCOME TAX ACT
speechtext: Can the minister not find out from his official?

maintopic: INCOME TAX ACT
speechtext: I will try to get that information and give it later in the day.

maintopic: INCOME TAX ACT
speechtext: Will the minister also give later in the day the other information I asked for, as to the number of investigating officials in connection with income tax in Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta? That should be readily available. I understand the total number is 332. I would also ask the minister to file a statement showing the amount of the assessments of income tax for farmers in the three western provinces, as well as the amount for the dominion. When the minister tells me he has not the figures in that form, all I can say is that I know the department has them; the minister must have been misinformed because the records are there.

maintopic: INCOME TAX ACT
speechtext: Let me correct my hon. friend. I said we had not those figures here. They are on record in the office.

maintopic: INCOME TAX ACT
speechtext: Will the minister also table that today?

maintopic: INCOME TAX ACT
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: INCOME TAX ACT
speechtext:
Have farmers in Ontario who failed to file their income tax returns within the specified time been visited by income tax officials and had their income arbitrarily assessed? I have heard that certain officials
Supply-National Revenue

representing the income tax department have gone to farmers and asked them for their bank pass books, and on the basis of the entries therein have arbitrarily assessed the farmers' income; and that in some cases the arbitrary assessment was considerably higher than it should have been.

maintopic: INCOME TAX ACT
speechtext:
There has not been any arbitrary assessment. Our inspectors have assisted the farmers in Ontario, as in the other provinces, in making their returns. In Ontario, inspectors both from the district office and from head office, French and English, have attended public meetings which were called in certain districts by the farmers themselves, and have there discussed the problems of the farmers with a view to giving them information which would assist them in making their returns.
I do not want the idea to go out that we are making victims of farmers. Here is the position. Income taxation started in 1917 and a great many of us did not like making out our returns then any better than the farmers do today who have only been making their returns for a year or two. But the law is the law and must be complied with.
What we have done to help the farmers is this. We have put out a book called The Farmer's Guide-one book for eastern farmers and another applicable to the particular type of farming that is done in the western provinces. This was done with a view to educating the farmers to keep records of their business done throughout the year. The farmers throughout Canada asked to be assisted as business people. Business people are compelled to keep records, and farmers should keep records, but the great majority of them keep no records. We are attempting to educate them to keep records. We have had many requests for this booklet, and have distributed 700.000 copies of it among the farmers throughout Canada in the last six or eight months.
I have heard of no great protest from the farmers themselves. On the contrary I have received many letters of commendation and thanks for the assistance that we have been attempting to give the farmers in keeping records of their business. But it is going to take a few years to educate the farmers, just as it did the rest of us, to keep records and play their part as other citizens do who are in business. We are not doing anything arbitrarily. We are handling the matter as tactfully as it can be handled, and I have no doubt that in two or three years we shall have obtained the results we expect.

maintopic: INCOME TAX ACT
speechtext: I appreciate the minister's reply. I was not trying to make the point that the farmers should not have to pay taxes. I believe that people in the farming industry ought to pay taxes as do people in other industries. But I do hope that the minister will continue along the line he suggested and make these forms as simple as possible. That is one of the main reasons why they object to filing them.

maintopic: INCOME TAX ACT
speechtext: It would take a Philadelphia lawyer to make them out now.

maintopic: INCOME TAX ACT
speechtext: That is it. The present form is more like the Domesday book, which was introduced into England by order of William the Conqueror, than a tax form. I hope that in the next two or three years everything possible will be done to make the form simpler.

maintopic: INCOME TAX ACT
speechtext: Work is progressing actively on the simplification of the forms. It might interest hon. gentlemen to know that the present form, complicated as it looks and is, is a better form than the one submitted by the Canadian federation of agriculture, because it is a more businesslike form.

maintopic: INCOME TAX ACT
speechtext: I want to follow up the answer given by the minister to the hon. member for Lake Centre. He said that 332 inspectors were out. That does not mean farm inspectors alone?

maintopic: INCOME TAX ACT
speechtext: No.

maintopic: INCOME TAX ACT
speechtext:
We should be given a breakdown, because the minister realizes that as the work is carried on there are different types of inspectors. There are those who deal entirely with farm returns, those who deal with business returns, and so on. Of the 332 inspectors we should be told how many are dealing with farm returns and how many are dealing with business returns.
I should like to endorse what the hon. member for Lake Centre said about the young people. That has been a bone of contention for a long while. These young people are actively assisting in the production of foodstuffs on the farm, and some consideration should be given to them. I hope something satisfactory can be worked out there. The minister was going to get us that information. We should get that information before the item passes.
I should like to deal with the Saskatoon mix-up. Will the minister give us the number of informations which were laid, the prosecutions which were started, the number that

Supply-National Revenue
were withdrawn and the number that were actually proceeded with?

maintopic: INCOME TAX ACT
speechtext:
The minister is quite right when he says that until two or three years ago farmers were never asked to pay income tax. This thing is quite new to them. The minister says that as years go by the farmers will become educated. I agree that the farmers are getting real education at the present time. The inspectors come around, compute their taxes for the past few years, and tell them that they have to come through with a payment, regardless of the conditions under which they live.
I should like to deal with two points. No farmer objects to paying a legitimate tax which is levied against him. I have not met a single farmer who objects to paying the same tax and on the same scale as anyone else pays who receives an income. What the farmers do object to is the arbitrary method of sending out inspectors who call at the home of the farmer and ask him what he was worth in 1940 or 1941 and what he is worth today, and then by simple subtraction telling him that he has to pay $1,000 or $2,000, or whatever it may be. In my own constituency farmers have been asked to pay more income taxes for the past three years than they are worth. That is unfair. Why did not the government tell the farmers that they were expected to keep books for 1941, 1942, 1943 and 1944? Not a word was said about income tax then. All of a sudden, after the election of 1945, these inspectors were sent out and told the farmer that he would have to produce his account books for 1941, 1942, 1943, 1944 and 1945. That sort of thing is unreasonable. It is something that should not be permitted to continue.
I appeal to the minister to instruct his officials-and I think it will pay not only the department but the country, and it will be the right thing to do-to forget about these back taxes. It would pay the country, even if we lost a little of the money that could be squeezed out of the farmers, if the income taxes for 1941, 1942, 1943 and 1944-that is, until the department actually issued instructions to collect these taxes-were permitted to fall by the wayside. I do not say that we should not collect taxes from farmers who are well off. Certainly if you can prove to the farmers that they did have income, why should they not pay? I am sure that they will not object; but this idea of slapping a few thousand dollars in a lump sum on a farmer is just the thing that is going to be unjust to the farmer. Furthermore-and I do not particularly object to this-it is going to sweep from western Canada the representatives of the minister's party, because the farmers feel that 5849-376
that is unjust, and that it is an unfair way of collecting taxes.

maintopic: INCOME TAX ACT
speechtext: They did not do it last Thursday.

maintopic: INCOME TAX ACT

maintopic: INCOME TAX ACT

Your party certainly
should not.

maintopic: INCOME TAX ACT
speechtext:
The fact remains that you cannot continue to enforce something that is unjust. I say to the minister that he is quite right; he is doing his job well. He is quite right in getting the tax that is levied upon the farmers for the years 1945, 1946, and up to the present time and the same would apply to the future. But he is not right when he sends out a bevy of inspectors who are chasing after the farmers from one end of western Canada to the other and telling them that they have to come through with income tax for 1941, 1942 and 1943. It is unfair.
The other day a farmer told me that he went to town to buy certain articles, and when he returned home he found that his wife and children were crying. He asked them what was the matter. His wife said that the income tax inspector was on the premises. She said that he had been terrible. The farmer asked where he was. She said, "If you go out to the pigpen you will find him. He is counting the pigs, but you will recognize him; he is wearing a hat."

maintopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Surely we are to have an explanation of the matter.
Mr. DONALD M. FLEMING (Eglinton): The Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin), as chairman on the special committee on prices, has moved that the house concur in the report which was tabled yesterday. It is my intention to review, as briefly as may be, some of the essential features of the report and some of the conclusions that flow from it.
In the first place I do not know how many members of the house have yet had the time or opportunity to read this report; it was distributed in mimeographed form late yesterday. It runs to something over seventy pages, and it may be that at this stage hon. members of the house have not had adequate opportunity to digest it. It is in the hope of assisting members that I desire to make some comments on the highlights of this report.
At the outset I point out that this is a majority report. When it was adopted at 1.30 a.m. yesterday by the committee, the motion for adoption was supported by the Liberal and C.C.F. members present at the time of the vote. It was opposed by the Progressive Conservative and Social Credit members.
The rise in the cost of living is a matter of general concern. Concern over the vaulting cost of living is not the exclusive right of any party or person in this house. It is a matter of the greatest concern to us all, just as it is a matter of lively concern to all Canadians.
The report contains some significant figures. The first appendix gives the figures on the rise in the cost of living in recent months. When the war ended the cost of living index stood between 118 and 120. At the end of May, 1948, the cost of living index was 153-3. The food index has shown an even more amazing climb. When the war ended the index was at a figure of approximately 135. At the end of May it had jumped to 191-2. We have in Canada today a condition of inflation-not of course in the sense of the inflation which Germany experienced after the first war, or the inflation of China today, but nevertheless a condition of inflation. Our Canadian dollar, in terms of purchasing powder compared with its

purchasing power before the war, is worth just two-thirds of w-hat it was then worth. Today we have a sixty-five cent dollar.
The government of course has misjudged the situation. Last October on his return from Europe, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott), at a time when the cost of living index stood at 138, said it was in the process of levelling off, that it would not go much higher, and that it was the expectation of the government that it would level off at not more than 145. I have already indicated, Mr. Speaker, that the index has continued to climb, and that at the end of May it had reached the figure of 153-3.
This committee in its majority x-eport has been busy tooting its own horn. You will find in not only one but sevei-al places in the report statements by the committee to the effect that it has conti-ibuted toward checking rises in the cost of living, that the mei'e fact that the committee has been sitting and has been conducting inquiries has resulted in people who have goods for sale taking lower prices than they otherwise would have taken. There may be the isolated case where that has happened, but in the approximately 4,000 pages of printed evidence taken by this committee, there just is not evidence that warrants such a finding.
The majoi-ity on the committee, the govei-n-ment membex-s, have been busy trying to keep up their courage by whistling. Apparently it was necessary in the government strategy, that any discussion on the question of the cost of living be kept off the floor of the House of Commons. And, of coui-se, the government majority on the committee has sought to justify the existence of the committee on some other basis. In all frankness I think the government majority might have said that was the purpose the committee could best serve.
However, I wish to comment briefly on the evidence as to the alleged usefulness of the committee. The one case to which the committee can point, where an individual said he was reducing the price of his product as the result of a request from the committee, was that of a baker in the city of Montreal, where aecoi'ding to my recollection he has one or two shops. He said he was going to reduce his bread from fourteen to thirteen cents a loaf. That was the only case; and on evidence of this kind the government majority on the committee purports to justify the existence of the committee and these four and a half months of sittings. It was a good advertising stunt on the part of that particular merchant. He obtained national advertising. I think it shows he was a realist and a good businessman, and that he really pulled the leg of my hon. friend the chairman of the committee.

Report of Prices Committee
However, the committee has seen fit to do something else. It has tried to justify its existence by the length of its report. So we have a report of almost prodigious length, measured in terms of what the committee has really accomplished; a report padded with repetitions. In other words, having little to show for its efforts, the committee has sought to write a long report to give the impression that the report has value.
Now I have some direct observations to make upon the report itself. The first observation is that the report was steam-rollered through the committee. Bear in mind, sir, that the committee continued its public sittings right up until Thursday noon of this week, and members of the committee saw the draft report for the first time Thursday morning. Several members were appointed a drafting committee and given copies of a draft report late the night before, too late to read it; but the committee sat down with a draft report in front of it for the first time on Thursday morning, a draft which was placed before us by the chairman and vice-chairman. The committee sat through the whole day, and at one-thirty Friday morning purported to adopt that report.
What was done at the meeting? There was discussion, a good deal of it; but in every case it came down to this: the opposition members on the committee were told, not once but repeatedly, that they might make observations, they might discuss the report, they might offer amendments, but unless those amendments were simply matters of dotting the i's and crossing the t's they would not pass. We were told that before we even began to discuss the amendments. You will realize, of course, Mr. Speaker, that as far as any participation by the members of the committee in writing that report went, what went on was little more than an empty formality. The essentials of the report were settled and determined before the committee ever saw it. When the report was submitted the committee was told that no amendment of substance would be tolerated.
Is this kind of procedure likely to elevate parliament, parliamentary institutions and parliamentary procedure in the minds of the public? I say that no tactic will more quickly and effectively undermine the confidence of the people in parliamentary institutions than steam-roller methods of this kind.
But that is not all. For several days past the press has in advance carried portions of the contents of this report. I am sure it must have shocked some members of the committee to find, when the report was finally submitted to them on Thursday, that it tallied verbatim with reports which had been appearing in, the
press for some days in advance, as to recommendations and statements the report would contain when made public. That is a shocking state of affairs, that the press or others should have access to a draft report, which was railroaded through a committee, before the members of that committee even had an opportunity of seeing it.
We find in this report what purport to be findings of fact. You will recall, Mr. Speaker, that in the resolution passed by this house last February the committee was given three tasks to perform. First, we were to find out the causes of the recent rise in the cost of living. Second, we were told to examine and report from time to time as to prices which had been raised above levels justified by increased costs. Third, we were to report upon rises in prices due to the acquiring or withholding from sale of goods by persons in excess of their own reasonable requirements.
These were the three tasks the committee was directed to perform. There is not time to review in detail what purport to be the findings of fact in this report. The committee was described by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) and others who participated in the debate in the house as a fact-finding body. I cannot go over the findings in detail, but I do wish, to comment briefly on them.
In the first place many of them are not according to the evidence. Others represent a lopsided, distorted and unfair presentation of the evidence. In the next place, the government majority on the committee has seen fit to turn this document into a vehicle of Liberal political propaganda. I am obliged to use the mimeographed copy of this report in referring to its contents; and I note on pages 14 and 15, for instance, that the government majority on the committee, the persons who really carried the report, though they were told to inquire into the causes of the recent rises in the cost of living, have seen fit to go back to the first great war, and to conjure up pictures of the relief lines in the days of depression. That is not the only evidence in this report that the government majority on the committee saw fit to turn it into a vehicle for political propaganda. There are many others, and I hope to have an opportunity of briefly indicating some of the more important examples.
Surely in a matter of this kind, where a parliamentary committee is purporting to reach findings of fact, parliament, or the committee in the first place, should make a complete statement of the facts and then reach a considered finding in reference to those facts. What has happened here? It has written page after page after page of general material in which expressions like this frequently occur:
5928	COMMONS
Report oj Prices Committee	____
"in certain lines of business" certain individuals and persons did certain things of which the committee does not approve.
Let me make this abundantly clear: wherever there was evidence before the committee that an individual was profiteering, then I say, with emphasis, that the committee should have said so and should have stated the facts on such things in detail, put them on the record, and reached its judgment about the individuals concerned. But that is not the way in which the majority on this committee has gone about its task. All the way through this report, in two-thirds of it, you will find this idea iterated and reiterated: that certain individuals in certain lines of business have done certain things-a general condemnation, without any attempt to separate those who were responsible for such things from those who were in no sense tarred with the brush of such actions.
This is an absolutely improper approach to the task. Where individuals have been responsible for lifting prices unwarrantably, those individuals should have been censured in this report. That is no excuse for a general smearing of all companies in any particular business. In that respect this report is a highly deplorable and incomplete document.
. The majority of the committee has been at great pains to find certain causes for the rise in the cost of living. Mr. Speaker, you will search in vain through the pages of this report for references to the extent to which government policies-many of them directly inflationary in their nature-have entered into the rise in the cost of living. Similarly you will search the pages of this report in vain for any reference to the extent to which government taxation has entered into the continually increasing cost of living.
Why is it that this report, which is so voluminous and so generous with its words in so many other respects, has seen fit, in the wisdom of the government majority, to maintain a most discreet and awesome silence on two of the leading causes for the rise in the cost of	living-inflationary	government
policies, and government taxation? It is in those respects and in others a woefully incomplete report of the proceedings of the committee. As a result there are certain aspects of it upon which I shall have to enlarge later, and I only mention that in passing.
When I come to what are called the conclusions in this report, hon. members will see why I say that the whole report bears clear evidence of the fact that on the part of the government majority it was written in a state of panic following three recent by-elections in

which the government candidates went down to defeat. It has been coloured for considerations of political expediency, on the part of the government majority.
We find at an early stage in the report what are described as conclusions. I have always thought it was usual to put the conclusions at the end of any document, but the committee has seen fit to put the conclusions at the beginning of the report. Why? Apparently the majority in the committee were very anxious that these conclusions at least should be read, even if people did not have the patience to go further into the report.
These "conclusions", sir, as you will note from reading the report, are recommendations; they are not conclusions at all. They are recommendations because they ask the government to do certain things. Why should these so-called conclusions appear, and by what name shall they be called? I propose to call them recommendations in the report, because that is the name given to them in the further supplementary estimates tabled in the house this morning. As item 934 we find an amount of $50,000 for the following:
To provide for the expenses of a commission to be appointed under part I of the Inquiries Act, to inquire into prices and related subjects, as recommended by the special committee on prices.
Therefore, with this approval in the government's further supplementary estimates, I choose to call these conclusions "recommendations". How does it come about that these recommendations appear in the report?
May I recall to members of the house the course of the debate which took place in the house early last February. We of the Progressive Conservative party said that the committee should have the power to make recommendations. We urged that. But what were we told? The Prime Minister had something to say about that, and the reasons why in his drafting of the resolution there had been no reference to any power to make recommendations.
At page 749 of Hansard for February 2 the hon. member for Lincoln (Mr. Lockhart) asked: "What about recommendations?" The Prime Minister in his answer said that so far as he was concerned the committee was not being given power to make recommendations, but that if they came back later and thought they should have the power to make recommendations, he would be prepared to treat sympathetically the request of the committee. From time to time in committee the subject of asking for power to make recommendations arose, but the committee did not place any motion of that kind before the house.

Report oj Prices Committee
Therefore it was with no little surprise that members of this committee found themselves confronted yesterday at 12:45 a.m. with a whole volume of recommendations. Bear this in mind, that everything the committee had done in four and a half months, sitting day in and day out, had been done on the basis that the committee was only a fact-finding committee and had no power to make recommendations. Many of us were surprised, indeed amazed, to find the press carrying a statement a few days before opposition members of the committee saw the draft report -a statement that the committee would make recommendations. We said it could not be so, because 'the committee had been told it had no such power.
It remained then for the vice-chairman of the committee, the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre (Mr. Maybank) to introduce in the committee this chapter of recommendations. It is worth remembering that it was this same hon. member who, when this matter was under debate in the house on February 3 last, said that Your Honour should rule out of order the Progressive Conservative amendment which sought to give power to the committee to make recommendations. He saw fit to say that the committee was to be a fact-finding committee, and that if it were given the power to make recommendations it would usurp the functions of the cabinet.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext: On a point of order, the hon. member is not quoting me correctly. If he desires to quote what I said in the house, I would request that he do it directly and not by paraphrase.

maintopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext:
It will give me very great pleasure to quote the hon. member's language in the house, as it is found at pages 819 and 820 of Hansard, where he deals with the amendment of my leader. The hon. member states that the effect will be to change the nature of the committee entirely from that of a factfinding committee, that the committee would then be advising on government policy. Then on page 819 the hon. member is reported as follows:
I submit that that procedure is quite foreign to the parliamentary system of this country.
He is referring to committees recommending matters of policy.

maintopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext: Read the amendment.

maintopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext:
I have been asked to read the amendment of my leader; I shall come back to that. The hon. member went on to say:
Government policy is to be designed by that committee which we commonly call the cabinet,
which has that responsibility and which must at all times have the confidence of the House of Commons. That in itself seems to me sufficient to require that a ruling should be given denying the validity of the amendment of the leader of the opposition.
What was that amendment? The amendment recommended that the said resolution be amended by inserting certain things, and then I come to the part that is of practical relevancy, which reads:
2. By adding at the end thereof the following clause:
"That as well as reporting its findings the committee shall from time to time make recommendations to the House of Commons, as in the opinion of the committee may be considered necessary to secure as far as possible fair and just returns to producers, employees and employers and fair and just practices in marketing and distribution that will safeguard the interests of consumers as well as of producers."
Bear in mind that the remark of the Prime Minister which I quoted had reference to recommendations in general. That remark was made in reply to a question which wTas asked before the amendment of my leader was introduced in the house.
The hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre went on to say-and I ask hon. members to bear his words in mind when reading the recommendations appearing in this report:
In addition to the fact that these amendments would direct the committee to be a policy-making body, thereby usurping the functions of the cabinet, they seek to put the committee in the position of recommending expenditures of public money.
And later on:
-and the advisability of reverting to the payment of subsidies, which, of course would also mean the payment of public money.
The report contains a recommendation for the payment of subsidies, one of the very things on which the hon. member sought to have that amendment ruled out of order. He continues:
A committee making a recommendation of that kind would be a body, not charged with the responsibilities of government, taking on the functions of government even to the extent of dipping into the public purse and directing expenditures therefrom.
And this is his parting shot:
All this, I submit, shows that these amendments are not designed only to give direction to a fact-finding body, but are designed to change the fact-finding body completely, making it a body which would have power to bring in recommendations on all manner of things, many of which could be relatively distant from the actual question of prices themselves, and very far afield from the original motion.
I do not know whether the hon. member regards himself as a prophet, but those words
Report of Paces Committee

of his are prophetic if you look at the recommendations that this committee has seen fit to bring in. I emphasize that the rules under which it proceeded, the whole basis of this inquiry of four and a half months was that it had no power to bring in recommendations.
These recommendations were submitted at the end of a long day; at exactly 12.45 a.m. they made their first appearance. When the government majority on the committee through the chairman and the vice-chairman saw fit to place in the hands of the members of the committee the draft report upon which the members were to pass, it did not include these recommendations. That part was held back until the conclusion of a long day at 12.45 on Friday morning. The recommendations were read then and put through in the space of minutes. I took objection on a point of order, and the chairman saw fit to overrule the objection. The rest of the committee were playing the game according to the rules that had been laid down by the house, but it remained for the government majority on the committee, backed by the ruling of the chairman, to change the rules in favour of government policy in the last half of the ninth inning of the game. There were two sets of rules, one for the opposition members of the committee, and -another set which was brought in during the dying minutes of the committee's sessions to suit the interests of the government.
Not only that; look at these recommendations. Some of them deal with matters that were never before the committee at all. The second one deals with the combines investigation commission, and suggests that the funds placed at its disposal are not sufficient. The commissioner was before the committee, and he did not say that he needed more money. Where that recommendation comes from, one does not know; but I do say that if money is needed to make the combines investigation commission more efficient for the purpose of finding evidence of combines that are inimical to the public interest through profiteering of any kind, then the house would be willing to authorize whatever expenditure might be required for that purpose. As I said, the commissioner said nothing about that, and it does not appear anywhere in the evidence.
Then we are asked to deal with such things as a uniform system of business accounting, which we are told has been advocated by various business associations in Canada. There is no evidence that came before the committee from business associations of Canada asking that a uniform system of business accounting be imposed by force of law on businesses in general. We heard about this for the first time when this recommendation appeared on our desks about one o'clock yesterday morning.
(Mr. Fleming.]
There is reference to rent controls. I am sure hon. members of the committee would have been very glad to consider the question of rent controls, but here we have a recommendation dealing with a matter on which the committee had no evidence. The only thing in regard to rent control that the committee heard about was whether controls on commercial accommodation should be continued or discontinued last March. We had no evidence at any time on the subject of the rent control of housing accommodation. It may be that the recommendation contains the substance of the views of practically all hon. members on this subject, but I am pointing out that this committee has brought in a recommendation on a matter in connection with which it had no evidence whatsoever.
I come to two other recommendations. One recommendation is for the removal of the excise taxes that rvere imposed as part of the government's restrictive program last November. It is a very sound recommendation; but where were the voices, during those many months from November, 1947, down to the present, of those hon. members who so glibly took up this proposal and hustled it through in the early hours of yesterday morning? They were the ones who stood up and supported the stand of the government in railroading those taxes through and imposing them by radio. At that time they saw fit to approve the principle of the imposition of taxes by radio. In this finding, commendable as it is, we see evidence that at last government members have wakened up, that at last they are beginning to pay some attention to the feelings of the people of this country with regard to these iniquitous taxes.
But that is not the only way in which the government members on this committee have in a practical way, whether they realized it or not, expressed themselves in terms of condemnation of government policy-of a government policy, incidentally, very stubbornly adhered to by this government. They say now that the government ought to give consideration to a relaxation of the import restrictions. It is the same thing again, Mr. Speaker. We of the official opposition-other opposition members can speak for themselves -fought these import restrictions on the basis on which they were imposed-yes, imposed by radio decree by the Minister of Finance. The government members on the prices committee should now be congratulated on having at least recovered a sense of reality, a sense of their obligation to the people.
In a word, sir, these recommendations, smuggled into the report in the dying moments of the session, show quite clearly that

Report oj Prices Committee
they have been written by political hands for a political purpose. This apparently is to be the new Liberal platform. It is hard to conceive of these recommendations being introduced by the chairman of the committee and the vice-chairman, themselves respectively a minister of the crown and his parliamentary assistant, without their having been carefully reviewed in advance and enjoying the doubtful distinction of cabinet approval. Whether that be so directly or not, we may be very sure that apparently here we have, in embryo form, the new platform which the Liberal party proposes to write at its forthcoming convention in August next.
I make this observation. It is quite clear that the person principally responsible for the drafting of the report-and I strongly suspect that it was the Minister of National Health and Welfare-has written it deliberately with a view to nudging over the C.C.F. so that the Liberal party can find a place well to the left of its present position. In many respects it has succeeded in out-C.C.F.'ing the C.C.F. That is no doubt the reason why the hon. member for Cariboo (Mr. Irvine), the C.C.F. member on the committee at the time the report was adopted, endorsed and voted for the report. If the government wants to write that kind of platform with that political view in mind, I suppose it has a right to do it, and the people will have an opportunity to judge just how much weight they should attach to recommendations of this kind, written to temper the winds of political expediency, and also apparently to take refuge from the winds of public disfavour as expressed in three recent by-elections.
I wish to make this general comment on the nature of the inquiry conducted by the committee. As a review of the price structure and as an investigation seeking to ascertain the reasons for the rise in the general price structure, it is woefully incomplete. I draw this to your attention, sir, that the committee dealt with only a few commodities. It investigated bread, butter, meats, fresh fruits and vegetables, and some textiles. In none of these cases did it investigate the commodity from the stage of its primary production until it is sold to the consumer. It took one stage, or at most two stages only. In the first place, I repeatedly asked the committee when it had completed its bread inquiry to bring in its report on bread. But government members said: Oh. no; it is not ready yet, because we shall have to go back and investigate the milling industry before we can complete our report on the bread industry. But the committee saw fit, through its government majority, to bring in its report yesterday without having made any investigation into the milling industry.
On butter we heard evidence from co-operatives, traders and storage warehouses, but not from retailers. On meats we heard from the packers, but not from wholesalers or retailers. On fresh fruits and vegetables we heard wholesalers, but nothing from retailers. On textiles we heard from primary manufacturers of three textiles, but we heard nothing about the intermediary stages before the textiles reach the ultimate consumer.
No attempt was made by the committee to seek a pattern of the price structure. These commodities we selected, were chosen largely because their prices were pressing on the consumer. These selections may have been sound, but I draw attention to this, that there is no ground for saying, as the report does say, that the committee has made a representative selection, or that it has found a pattern; for the committee has not touched on other foods, nor has it inquired into clothing, boots and shoes, fuel, and many other commodities.
To illustrate hotv incomplete an inquiry of this kind was from the point of view of getting at the nub of the problem, which is the price paid by the consumer, I draw this to your attention, Mr. Speaker: that in our inquiry into the prices of wool-. It has just been intimated to me, sir, that you are about to rule that I am under a time limit. I shall have to argue against it if you make that ruling. I am far from finishing the main portion of my speech, and I consider that on a government motion moved by a minister I am under no time limit.
But I had better put my amendment on record now. I move, seconded by the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard (Mr. Merritt):
That the said report be not concurred in but that the same be referred back to the special committee on prices for the purpose of amending it by deleting the conclusions therein and substituting therefor the following conclusions:
(a)	That the government should give consideration to the immediate removal of all special excise taxes levied and collected as from November 18, 1947;
(b)	That the government should give consideration to immediately exempting from sales tax and excise tax all articles that enter into the family budget;
(c)	That the government should give consideration for the benefit of those in the lower income groups to immediately reducing the income tax and increasing the exemptions;
(d)	That positive and practical steps be taken forthwith to eliminate extravagance and thereby reduce the cost of government;
(e)	That in the opinion of the committee the continuing increased cost of living and rising prices are substantially attributable to the government's inflationary policies.
It is my purpose now to review the reasons for this amendment.
