maintopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext:
May I thank the house for its courtesy. I assure you, sir, that I shall endeavour to conclude my remarks as quickly as I can.
I was dealing with the point that the committee had touched only part of the problem of the rise in prices. The thing that we are concerned with is the rise in prices to the consumer. To show how incomplete has been an inquiry of this kind from the point of view of arriving at conclusions as to the reasons for the rise in general price structure, I mention these facts brought out in evidence.
Our inquiry into the price of wool showed that the amount to which the increase in the price at the manufacturing level, the primary producer's level, contributed to the cost to the consumer is only fractional; but the clothing cost index shows this, and these are government figures: in March, 1947 the level was 133-1. In March, 1948 it was 169-9, a rise in that year, sir, of 36-8 points. But look at what has been contributed !by the primary producer toward this price rise. The amount that would be contributed by the manufacturer to the cost of a man's suit of clothes would be just $3 in that year. Everybody knows how much the price of men's clothes has gone up in that period. But at the manufacturer's level, which is the only one the committee dealt with, the rise would amount to only S3 in the price of the suit. On an overcoat, only $3 of the total rise was accounted for in that way. According to my recollection the figure was S1.40 on a topcoat. If 3'ou will pardon this illustration, in the case of ladies' hosiery we were told that the proportion of increase in cost that could be attributed to the primary manufacture level, with which we were dealing, was sixteen cents a pair. Where do we find the reasons for the rise in the cost to the consumer of the remainder which is the great bulk of the rise in the cost to the consumer, which has, so far as the committee's study is concerned in its report, remained an unanswered question, an unfathomed problem? In the result, sir, I have to say this, that the committee, based on a partial survey of some aspects of half a

Report of Prices Committee
dozen commodities in the country, has seen fit to try to exempt the government from blame that properly attaches to government policy for much of the rise in the cost of living.
The government, sir, had the powers to deal with this problem. It had the law at its back, because the wartime prices and trade board general order, to which the house gave the force of a statute a year ago last March, specifically makes it an offence under the law of this country to charge for any commodity a price that is higher than just and reasonable; or to accumulate goods in excess of those required by the individual responsible for his own reasonable purposes. The Bank of Canada was available to the government, and according to the stated purpose in the preamble to the act, it was to be available to eliminate the humps and hollows in general business conditions. The powers of the Bank of Canada were available to try to prevent runaway prices. Then, there is the combines investigation commission with very wide powers. And lastly, but by no means least, there is the power of the government to use the taxing power either for the purpose of taxation or for the purpose of exempting from taxes as the case may be. In every one of those cases the use made by the government of its powers has not been, in my submission, to contribute to a reduction in the runaway cost of living.
May I just mention quickly one or two examples?-because I am trying to hurry along. Take fresh fruits and vegetables. Until the government on November 17 last imposed an embargo on the importation of certain vegetables and restricted the import of certain fruits and put a complete embargo on others, their prices had not soared, but then overnight there grew up a consumer's panic, and prices soared. At or about the end of February or the first of March the government saw fit to impose a price ceiling on these vegetables which were in such short supply, a situation which the Canadian producer was in no position to meet at that time of the year; and the committee, sir, has the audacity to commend the government for acting promptly in that situation, after they had sat back, after creating the condition on November 17 in which these prices soared almost overnight, sat back for three months before they moved to check the runaway prices of those commodities.
As to the Bank of Canada, the evidence given before the committee by Mr. Towers did not leave very much hope that the powers assigned by statute to the Bank of Canada will be used to check this runaway 5849-377
cost of living. Mr. Towers said in effect that, apart from drastic action of the kind that he apparently was not prepared to contemplate, the only thing that the Bank of Canada could do to end it was done, namely, to ask the chartered banks in March of this year to tighten up on loans to commercial enterprises. That is all. In the light of the evidence, it would appear that the powers of the Bank of Canada are not available to be used to check the things that have contributed, within bank policy and government policy with which it is allied, to the increase in the cost of living and the increase in the price level.
In the light of the amendment-and I am trying to hurry now-I shall touch on this question of taxation as it enters into the cost of commodities. In this respect the committee had some evidence before it. But the majority on the committee in this case has seen fit to ignore completely the evidence on this point, has seen fit to ignore completely this entire subject and to write a report that is silent as to the place of taxation; although, may I remind you, Mr. Speaker, that they slipped into the body of recommendations a recommendation for which you will find no counterpart in the pages and pages of narrative in the report.
On the subject of taxation we of the Progressive Conservative party hold the view, as to indirect taxes, that because they are passed on to the consumer, they contribute to increasing the cost to the consumer. That is the nature of the tax. An indirect tax is one that is passed on, by the person on whom it is imposed in the first instance, to the ultimate consumer. You see that in the case of the sales tax and the excise tax. They are passed on and they pyramid as they go on. A year ago I gave the house the instance of stockings that started out at a price of SI a pair when produced by the manufacturer, bearing an eight per cent sales tax at that point but which had pyramided, by the time the stockings had passed through the hands of the wholesaler, the jobber and the retailer and reached the consumer, to a tax of not eight per cent but 14-8 per cent. All kinds of instances of that sort can be found in which the tax pyramids to a greater height than that.
Then I wish to refer to the subject of direct taxation, and when I do so I am thinking of taxes like the income tax. We say that is a tax which bears heavily on the individual pocketbook and is one that cries for remedial action in times like these; because taxes of that kind should be reduced in times like these in order to come to the rescue of the man who is caught between
Report of Prices Committee

the upper and nether millstones of limited income and this rising cost of living.
The government had a great opportunity to use its direct tax policies in a remedial way to meet the exigencies of the hard-pressed taxpayer, above all, those in the lower income brackets, by reducing the tax and by increasing exemptions. In saying that I wish to be quite clear. We of this party have supported the principle of reasonable budget surpluses in good times, but we have said that surpluses of the kind budgeted for this year bear no resemblance to reasonableness under conditions like these, where so many people with small incomes are having such a desperate time today to meet the cost of living.
What has been the government's tax policy? Let me say just a word first as to the excise taxes imposed last November. They were imposed in many cases on the necessities of life; and now, after we heard last Tuesday from the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) a statement that there is no truth in the newspaper reports that the government was proposing to lift the excise taxes which were imposed last November, we find this committee bringing in by a side wind a recommendation directly on that point.
Let no one think the removal of the excise taxes or the other indirect taxes like the sales tax, which applies still to too many items that enter into the cost of living of the average Canadian family, would not reflect itself in a reduced cost of living. Let me just remind you, Mr. Speaker, and the house of what happened last November when the government brought in these increases in taxes. It added for a little sugar-coating a couple of reductions in taxation, one of them being the reduction in the tax on electricity. What happened? The dominion bureau of statistics reflects the fact that, in the month following the removal of that electricity tax, there was an astonishing effect on the cost of electricity to the consumer, the Canadian family. According to the statistics reported by the dominion bureau of statistics, fuel and light for the month-that is, the month following November 18-^showed an actual drop of 2-3 points. Is there any reason to doubt that, if the government would remove other indirect taxes, the consumer would enjoy a similar reduction in the cost of living?
If it is the intention of the government really to take seriously the recommendation of the committee in this respect, then let them not boggle about it; let them not try to preserve face by purporting to adopt a recommendation from a committee. Let them

boldly take action now and remove these taxes while parliament is in session. Let them bring in their bills now for the removal of these taxes. Away with the excise tax imposed last November! Away with the sales tax as far as it applies to all the commodities that enter into the family budget of the Canadian family! Away with all the other excise taxes that apply to many of these necessities of life which have a direct bearing on the cost of living to the Canadian family!
On the subject of taxes, Mr. Speaker, let me tell you that the committee had some evidence on this point. Here is the evidence given by one of the textile manufacturers who was before the committee. This presentation was filed with the committee just within recent days. This company, Canadian Celan-ese Limited, shows in its breakdown of taxes that no less than 15-9 per cent of its total dollar volume of sales goes to pay taxes; and of that, 12-8 per cent goes to pay dominion taxes. If we are looking for some opportunity to bring the cost of living down closer to the capacity of the Canadian people to pay, let the government take immediate action to reduce these taxes the Canadian consumers are paying, because they are being paid by the Canadian consumer. I refer to these indirect taxes; and I ask the government also, even at this late date in the session, to deal with the question of trying to preserve to the Canadian of small income the proportion of his income which they are taking now in income taxes and which he badly needs to meet the increases in the cost of living.
Lastly, Mr. Speaker, I wish to refer to controls; and I do not intend to take time to go into the whole subject. I should have liked to have time to deal with them and to read extracts from the evidence on the matter. We had much evidence on the subject of controls, and we had from Mr. Graham Towers the statement that the country cannot expect to use controls to cope with the general rise in the price level unless it is prepared to apply a general over-all price control policy. He said that control would have to include wages and salaries, and would have to be a far more rigid over-all control than existed in time of war. He also recognized that it would have to be generally acceptable to the Canadian people and have their strong support. Otherwise, Mr. Speaker, as you know, you would have the black market running wild.
Similar things were said by Mr. Taylor, chairman of the wartime prices and trade board, the man closer to the enforcement of controls than any other person in Canada, as to the impossibility of maintaining a general over-all price control or of reimposing such

Report of Prices Committee
controls today. I asked what would happen if today the government sought to push back prices, as parliament is sometimes invited to dio, to the 1946 level. His reply was, "Complete chaos." I asked why, and his .answer was simply that the primary producer just would not produce, because he will not produce unless there is a profit incentive for him. If you are going to talk about pushing back prices and enforcing a rigid over-all price control policy, then, according to Mr. Kenneth Taylor, you will just not get production.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I say the problem, in the last analysis being one of scarcity, will be solved only by greater production. That will be the only final solution. Anything that stands in the way of production; anything that results in production being curbed or discouraged. is directly contributing to inflation in Canada. Among those things which are causing inflation are these government policies which are having the effect of discouraging production.
The Progressive Conservative party does not [DOT]believe that the way out of the problem of a rising level of prices is to grind down the farmer. Today the farmer is simply enjoying rights which he has been denied for a long time. He has not hitherto been receiving fair play, and we of the Progressive Conservative party will oppose any policy that denies the primary producer the fair fruits of his labours.
Nor are we prepared to support any government policy that will have the effect of increasing bureaucracy in Canada and of imposing controls that have as their ultimate effect a restriction of production. If we follow policies that restrict, policies that control, which will have the effect of discouraging production, then our last state will be worse than our first.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I submit that the course which ought to be followed right now by this government is to do away with these taxes which have done so much to raise the cost of living, taxes which, with the increased prices, have themselves risen in amount because they are percentage taxes, and these income taxes that are taken from the pockets of the people, money they badly need to meet this increased cost of living. And, sir, this government should abandon the policies I have referred to, which have had the effect of restricting production and discouraging the producer.

I should like to raise a point of order in regard to the amendment. The house may direct a committee as to what it is to inquire into. It may enlarge the order of reference by means of an instruc-5849-3771
tion, but it cannot tell a committee in advance what it must find. That is what this amendment seeks to do. It states:
That the said report be not concurred in but that the same be referred back to the special committee on prices for the purpose of amending it by deleting the conclusions therein and substituting therefor the following conclusions. . .
In other words, by this amendment the house would be telling a committee which it had appointed to inquire into a matter what its conclusions must be. Here are five findings that are to be made by the committee. Surely a motion to that effect is entirely out of order.
I would refer as well to standing order 65, section 2:
(2) It shall always be understood that no member who declares or decides against the principle of a bill, resolution, or matter to be committed, can be nominated of such committee.
Here my hon. friend has already decided against the matters that are to be referred to the committee, and has indicated what the committee is to find. According to the rules governing the setting up of a committee, he could not even be a member of it. Obviously the amendment is out of order.

maintopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE

I have no particular reason for wishing the motion to be declared in order, but I would refer to Beauchesne, third edition, page 204, citation 570, where I find these words:
When the motion to concur is proposed the report may be referred back to the committee for further consideration or with instruction to amend it in any respect. It is not competent for a committee to reconsider and reverse its own decision, but if the house resolves that such reconsideration is necessary, the correct procedure is for the house to give the committee instructions which will enable it to consider the whole question again.
The committee is not dealing with this matter; it is being dealt with by the house at the moment.

maintopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I had not thought I would be speaking at this juncture, after the compelling criticism that has been leveled at the government in connection with this report. I should have expected them to make some attempt to defend themselves following the brilliant speech by the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming) to which we have just listened. From the unwillingness of any hon. member on the other side of the house to make an attempt at least to justify what the
Report of Prices Committee

government and the maj ority on this committee have done, I feel one is led to the conclusion that they cannot make any defence, that they have none to offer.
In view of that fact, and in view of the lateness of the session I hope I shall not speak at any great length. However, as seconder of the amendment whose fate you have just taken under consideration, Mr. Speaker, I think I should address a few remarks to the house. I sat as a member of this committee since its inception in February, and during the course of such lengthy hearings one cannot help but form some conclusions.
I do not want to repeat anything that has been so ably said by the hon. member for Eglintoni with regard to the way in which the deliberations of the committee were conducted, but I must make a few remarks with respect to the fourteen recommendations brought before the committee about one o'clock yesterday morning. The hon. member for Eglinton has pointed out how some of them are critical of the government and critical of the government's policies. Six of them are directly critical of the government. Four more are innocuous enough as recommendations, and will have no effect at all in reducing prices. There is another series of four which I think one could describe as the ash-can sections, because each one of them has in its wording the obvious way in which it can be thrown into *the ash-can as soon as the house rises.
I wish to protest against any idea that I *was a party to any of those recommendations. I was a member of the committee, so far as the rest of the report was concerned. Although I did not concur in it, and was opposed to it, nevertheless the rest of the report refers to the work of the committee. But this part II of the report, as I call it, the conclusions or recommendations, is not even the recommendations of the majority of the committee. They are the recommendations of a group of Liberal members on the committee, headed by one of the cabinet ministers. They are inspired, not so much from the evidence adduced before the committee, but from' the dissatisfaction of those members with the policies of the government. While the main part of the report can be called the report of the committee on prices, I can only call these fourteen conclusions or recommendations the second Brei'thaupt report. If they are not that, then, as the hon. member for Eglinton says, they are a preview of a Lansdowne park platform in August.
I wish to make it perfectly clear and plain that, as a member of the committee, I resented the attempt to make me a party to the washing of dirty cabinet linen in public; because

when we consider that the recommendations -of which the six most important are directly critical of the policies followed by the government-were brought in at this last moment by a member of the cabinet, we can only reach the conclusion that there is a split in the cabinet, and that that split in the cabinet is having a lot to do with the difficulties of this country in facing our present problems, particularly the problem of the rising cost of living.
It is interesting to see what those six recommendations are. There is the recommendation that the import restrictions be relieved. There is the recommendation that the excise tax be removed. There is the recommendation for a change in rental controls, and then there is the recommendation which is perhaps more important than all the others in its application to the great clambake which will take place in August, namely recommendation No. 12, which contains the veiled suggestion that the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) should not be allowed to proceed with his announced policy with regard to the export embargo on cattle.
Some of these are proper recommendations to make. I believe we have advocated all of them but the last from this side of the house right through the session. Furthermore we voted against the introduction of the policies about which the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin) is now complaining. But there is just one thing I would say to him, and that is that he should fix up those things on his own side of the house, and not try to use a committee-at least not one of which I am a member-to fry his fish.
With regard to the rest of the report let me point out that this is a political document entirely; it is not a contribution to the understanding by the Canadian people of the causes of price increases in this country. It could not be considered an attempt at enlightenment of the public. It is a verbose document, and it is inconclusive because it was insufficiently considered.
Right through the course of the investigation, as a member of the committee I have taken the position that we should not load ourselves with so much work that we could not bring in some useful findings with respect to matters which we were investigating. And when we come up to just the day before yesterday-almost the last day of the session- and have thrust before us this long sixty-page report, which took all day to read, let alone to consider, one can see what very little consideration was given to the report by the committee.

Report of Prices Committee
I have no doubt that a great deal was thought, of it by the Minister of National Health and Welfare, or whoever was its author. But the committee itself had practically no chance to consider it at all. It does not represent a serious attempt to convey to the Canadian people the reasons for the rising cost of living.
I should like to make another general observation about the report and about the work of the committee. I was greatly impressed by the fact, which was brought out time and again in evidence, that the government had, without the committee, all the means at its disposal whereby it could get the information it wanted and could take the action it wanted.
We had before us some of the senior officers of the government-some very able men, indeed. We had before us Mr. Taylor, chairman of the wartime prices and trade board; Mr. Graham Towers, and many other officers in government departments. Their evidence was most helpful. Indeed I believe it was tfle most important evidence we heard, because they knew, and they told us, why the cost of living had been going up-and they had certainly long before told the government the same things as they told us.
I was greatly interested in one bit of evidence given by Mr. Taylor. The press of this country during the sittings of the committee had a lot to say about the high profits made by companies engaged in the selling of butter. It came like a bolt from the blue. The evidence of Mr. Taylor was that he knew of these butter profits long before the committee was set up, away back at the beginning of *December when he was having one of his periodic conferences with the dairy industry. Information about the rise in the price of butter during the fall was known to the government, and yet no action was taken by the government upon that information. It did not need this committee to bring out information with respect to the butter situation; the government knew of it all the time.
It is interesting to note that there were officials of the government very close to the meat situation. They had to be, because the government is in the meat business. There was nothing discovered by this committee that those officials did not know. There was not one bit of that evidence that required the actions of this committee to elicit. I have no doubt that the purpose of setting up the committee was simply to turn pressure away from the government in the house.
When we turn to the report we find that it is completely unbalanced. It is so unbalanced that it is clear it is designed only as an attempt to exonerate the government from
responsibility for rising prices. This was a serious committee set up to find out why these prices were rising. We spent ninety-five per cent of our time in investigating the activities of firms in a few lines of business. We spent very little time and gave very little consideration to the much more important problems that are behind the activities of those firms in their various fields.
I suggest that the kind of problem we should have been studying was the relative positions of production and consumption of the goods in Canada which enter into the cost of living. We should have been finding out whether we had enough production and, if not, why not. We should have been trying to see that production was increased. We should have been examining into the question of consumption, and we should have brought in a report to the house showing how these two vital problems contribute to a rise in the cost of living. The fact that we did not go into those fundamental things; the fact that we dismissed them with a few hours of evidence and with a few words in the report shows how political a document this is and how it was not really an attempt to grapple with the problem.
I should like to speak for a few minutes with reference to the last paragraph of the amendment moved by the hon. member for Eglinton, which reads:
That in the opinion of the committee the continuing increased cost of living and rising prices are substantially attributable to the government's inflationary policies.
There is no direct reference in the report to the influence of government policy on the price level, but in the recommendations of the Minister of National Health and Welfare government policies are inferentially deemed to have made such a contribution to the cost of living. After hearing evidence on the prevailing price levels of a number of commodities, I am of the opinion that those levels were the direct result, or one might even say the considered aim, of government policies.
Mention has been made of the high rate of taxation, of the twenty-three cents in the dollar which goes to the dominion government in taxes these days. Mention has been made of the sales tax and of the easy-money policy of this government which contributed to the increase of purchasing power in Canada, one of the causes of rising prices as found by the committee.
When you come to examine the various commodities dealt with you find a most extraordinary thing. In some cases the domestic wholesale price was fixed by the government, either directly or indirectly, and
Report oj Prices Committee

in other cases there was a direct connection between government policy and the increase in the price. Let me just deal with the commodities we did examine.
In the case of butter we had evidence that the wholesale price had gone up to between sixty-nine and seventy cents at the time the ceilings were put on. We had evidence that the wartime prices and trade board were instructed early in December to consider the price at which they would reimpose the ceiling. We had evidence from Mr. Taylor that they could not make that decision until they knew what price would be fixed by the government for the export of cheese to Great Britain. When they knew that price at the end of December they were able to put on the ceiling of sixty-seven cents.
We had evidence that the price of butter is directly related to the export price of cheese and that if the prices board had fixed the ceiling price of butter below two and one-eighth times the export price of cheese there would have been no 'butter production in Canada. In effect, the government put a floor price of sixty-seven cents under butter, and the price we are now paying in Canada is a direct result of government policy.
Similarly with meat. We had evidence which showed that by far the largest rise in the price of pork, namely, four cents from seventeen to twenty-one cents a pound, occurred on January 1, 1947. That price rise immediately followed the negotiation of the new export bacon contract. We had evidence at the same time that the increase in the price of pork caused buyers to increase their consumption of beef, thereby sending beef prices upward. There again a floor price was put under these commodities by the government, and the price of meat as it is today is the direct result of government policy. If the people of Canada are complaining about those prices, they know precisely where to place the responsibility.
With regard to fruits and vegetables, it was only too clear that prices rose as they must when you cause a scarcity condition in any commodity. It was inevitable that the import restrictions on fruits and vegetables would bring about exactly what happened. Although there were cases of high prices and very large profits among fruit and vegetable dealers which should be condemned, the fact remains that it was the policy and the action of this government in imposing import restrictions which made it possible for these things to be done, and it is idle to criticize a few individuals for what they did when the certain result of their policies could easily have been foreseen by the government.

I conclude my remarks by referring to the last recommendation of the committee, No. 14, which reads as follows:
The committee wishes to emphasize the fact that increased production at home and abroad is the only permanent solution to the problem of high prices. The present shortage of commodities is world-wide, forcing world prices to high levels, which in turn are forcing Canadian prices upward.
There it is pointed out, and of course it is true, and we did not need a committee to tell us, that it is production and production alone which can bring prices down. WThen considering how far the government is responsible for rising prices I think it is a fair question to ask, what is their record in the stimulation of production? I think we shall find that, far from having any clear policy designed to increase the production of goods in Canada, the government have taken every step they could to restrict production and dam it back and to interfere with the abundant flow of goods in Canada, It is those restrictive policies, which I know the government say have been forced upon them by events, which day by day are becoming more and more responsible for rising prices in Canada.
We shall never have increased production if we maintain the present rate of taxation. Everyone knows that. The government know it just as well as I do, but they have not been able to stop their extravagance and get our taxes down. In the committee we saw the direct relationship between import restric-ions and prices. That was evident in the fruit and vegetables field. There is no doubt in my mind that the government's import restrictions are contributing greatly to increased prices in Canada today. At the same time, under the policies of the foreign exchange control board we are stifling the entry of capital into Canada and making it more difficult than ever to import goods and to increase the supply of goods in this country. We have heard in recent months in this house the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) and the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) say over and over again that Canada's capital goods development is placing so great a strain upon our supply of manpower and materials that it is necessary to cut it back and not to spend so much money on capital development. We have the Canadian dollar maintained at par under the foreign exchange control board. The import restrictions on goods and the maintenance of the Canadian dollar at an unreal figure are two ways of creating scarcity in Canada and consequent rising prices. Rising prices must be the inevitable result of the continuation of these policies, and we shall

Report of Prices Committee
never get out of our present situation unless those policies are reversed.
I was most interested to read in the press the other day that the president of the New York curb exchange had visited western Canada and looked over various opportunities there. He was quoted as saying: "You have plenty of opportunities in this part of the country, and we have plenty of capital in the United States seeking a profitable outlet, but you cannot expect capital to walk into a trap." That is the situation brought about by the government's exchange policy. It has stopped the influx of capital which in turn would have enabled us to increase our importation of capital goods and would have lessened the pressure of purchasing power on the price of all other goods that we have in the country or that we wish to import. If, Mr. Speaker, the government should find some way of attracting capital into Canada the import restrictions could be taken off in a moment.
I point out to the government, who are so fearful of an adverse balance of trade with the United States that we must restrict everything we do, that until 1920, for the first fifty years in the life of Canada we had in almost every year, not only an adverse balance of trade with the United States but an over-all adverse balance of trade.
We were always importing more than we exported of our own production. In none of those years was it necessary to put on import restrictions to create scarcities in Canada and to cause our prices to rise in a way to distress our people. In each of those years people abroad, having confidence in Canada and realizing that it was a country in which it was safe and wise and profitable to invest their money, came in here and added to our store of foreign exchange with their own savings. By that action we were enabled to build up the productive forces which we have in Canada today and of which we are so proud.
The Minister of Finance and the Minister of Trade and Commerce have complained about our tight manpower situation. They have suggested that, since we have full employment, the only way to improve our present difficulties is to put on excise taxes and to cut back consumption and production. Why should we cut back production and consumption because we have full employment? Why should we not go after the manpower bottleneck, step up our immigration program and, alongside of new capital, bring in the new people to work in Canada to enable us to get after this production which the minister recommends so strongly?
In the first four months of this year, according to figures given in the house the other day, only 32,500 people came into Canada; I do
not know how many left. That is at the gross rate of 100,000 a year. Well, Mr. Speaker, in the great days of this country when we were trying to go ahead instead of to cut back, when we thought a rise in prices was a sign of prosperity instead of a thing we should shrink from, we had 200,000, 300.000 and 400,000 people coming to Canada every year. We had the money coming in with them to assist us in putting these new Canadians to work. We had prosperity all round and a happy and contented people, not a people worrying as to where they would get their next day's supply of bread and butter.
What I dislike particularly about the restric-tionist policy of the government is this. If ever I learned anything while sitting on the committee on prices I learned that the policies of this government in cutting off the flow of goods in Canada, in cutting back production and in attempting at the same time to reduce our consumption by these various control measures which we all know so much about this session, are bound to lead to further reduc- . tion in production and further rises in prices. So long as you stop goods coming in; so long as you stop the increase of our production facilities; so long as you keep this country with a manpower shortage and allow in only a trickle of people every year, so long will you keep your high prices. It is time that the government completely swallowed themselves and reversed their policies. It is time they stopped excessive taxation; it is time they stopped restricting trade; it is time they stopped stifling capital development, and it is time they went after the manpower shortage instead of sitting back and saying that because we have not the people we cannot do anything in this country.
In spite of the recommendations and conclusions in this report, I suggest that we pay no attention to it. I suggest that we set the dollar free, that we set trade free, that we set the Canadian people free to go about production in Canada in their own way and as they see fit. I suggest that we make this country a mecca for all free people who are vigorous and want to work, who want to have opportunity. Then we shall have production, and when we have production we shall have reduction in prices.
In these days we have an opportunity of gathering our forces together to go on to be a great nation. The test of whether we have a good government in Canada is whether people outside our borders who have money to invest, or who want a future in a country of opportunity, are looking to Canada as a place where they want to invest their money or to make that future. If you have an inflow of capital and people, then you have a good

government. If you do not have these two things; if you dry them up, you have a bad government. Anyone who knows about the figures of immigration of people or capital today knows we have a bad government now.

I agree also with him when he says we did not get very far. We concluded just about the time we should have been beginning. We have not even scratched the surface of the job that was given to us. So we can only speak of the very limited field which we have covered.
The point I would make in that connection is that the basic industries were never touched at all, even though they have both a direct and an indirect effect upon all the commodities that we were trying to study. The price of steel, the price of gasoline and of other commodities all have their effect on the price of bread, and even on the price of butter. But we made no examination into that. We plunged right into butter and pretty nearly stayed there most of the time. The investigation was lacking in thoroughness there, but that was not the fault of the committee. I think it will be agreed that we did all that any committee could have done with such a subject in the time we had at our disposal.

I want to make a comment or two on the findings of the committee with respect to the causes of higher prices. The factors of significance which were regarded as being causal of high prices, in the findings of the committee, were: first, the rise in external prices, that is to say, prices in countries other than Canada with which we must deal; second, the increase in costs of production; and third, the expansion of purchasing power in relation to the goods and services available. I want to make a comment on each of these alleged causes.
With regard to external prices, it is clear that Canada's prices have been rising for some time. Our price rises in Canada become external prices to other countries, causing them in turn to raise their prices still higher because our prices went up. Our relationship in that respect to other nations is pretty much that of an industry in Canada to inter-related industry, and so the spiral will continue just because we have allowed our prices to rise higher and become external prices to other countries.
As to the increase in production costs, I think we begged the question there, because it is more than likely that any increase in production costs must have been caused by the increased prices of certain materials which enter into costs, and not having found what made those prices rise, we should not just assume that there was an increase in costs of production which caused the recent price increases. I think that is begging the question.
As to the third factor, the expansion of purchasing power, I am hoping that the hon. member for Lethbridge (Mr. Blackmore) or some of his associates will enlighten us on that. The purchasing power abroad in this country today is alleged to be more than is necessary to purchase the goods that are available on the market. I believe that the hon. member for Lethbridge and his associates would like to have still more purchasing power distributed. However, they will be able to deal with that point. Of course there can be no doubt that the expansion of purchasing power is a vital factor, and we cannot afford to ignore it, whether it is raised by the hon. member for Lethbridge or in the report of the prices committee. There is a vital connection between the amount of money in circulation at any time and the amount of goods on the market to be
bought, and these factors in a society such as ours must have a direct bearing on prices and cause them to go higher or lower as the case may be.
Having found these causes, the committee should, I suggest, have been vested with sufficient power to make recommendations on howto cope with the effects which we have noted until the causes could be removed, and secondly, to advise how this parliament should proceed to remove the causes of high prices.
I think it will be agreed that the most important point in the causes is the implied shortages in relation to effective demand. I am almost afraid to use the words "supply and demand"; we heard so much of them in the committee. There supply and demand were more or less represented by those who talk so much of it as a law of peerless perfection, which works in such a way that supply is always demanded and demand is always supplied. But that just does not happen, or there would have been no need for the committee.
The question is this, as I see it: Shall we use wisely the principle of supply and demand, or shall we allow the undirected principle of supply and demand to use us? Demand, properly understood, is the measure of a nation's capacity to consume goods; that is the sum total of any rational demand. Supply is the measure of a nation's capacity to produce the goods demanded. These two factors, if used wisely in a planned economy, would be safe guides to our economic policy. But demand in a private enterprise economy means the measure of the total monetary income of would-be consumers, and supply means the measure of what it is profitable to produce. Both supply and demand are hampered by a private enterprise economy. I must not stop to develop that because I see my time is running out.
Everyone knows that shortages in essentials such as food, clothing, homes, and the like will mean higher prices in a competitive market under our present system of private enterprise. That is precisely the first problem with which we have to deal. That was the problem to which the committee had to address itself; for, even if a fuller production were achieved so that shortages were in part at least abolished, the best way of reducing prices would still have to be given consideration, because the need for price controls continues to exist up to the point where shortages cease. Shortages will unquestionably send prices up until only those who have the money can buy, and those who have not the money will not be able to buy. That will, of course, shorten the demand and start us down the hill, and that is where
Report of Prices Committee

you begin to move on toward the next committee which will be dealing with how to raise prices.
We had similar shortages during the war and we dealt with them. This government dealt with them in a manner which I think met with the general approval of the people of Canada, to a great extent at least. We found, during the war, that prices would not go down voluntarily; that nobody intended to bring them down voluntarily. The fact is that prices rose during the war in spite of patriotic fervour, and, but for controls, would have skyrocketed. So that if prices were not reduced voluntarily in time of war, we may be sure that will not happen in time of peace. I want to quote in that regard Mr. F. A. McGregor, combines investigation commissioner, who said this at page 157 of the report:
Under our wartime price legislation the freedom of individual sellers to decide their own prices was sharply curtailed. It had to be, because we were living in a period of serious shortages. Under such conditions competition was not the appropriate public safeguard.
There is also the observation of Mr. K. W. Taylor, chairman of the wartime prices and trade board, who said at page 58 of the evidence:
Shortages . . . are numerous and widespread and some of them are severe ... A 5 or 10 per cent shortage can drive prices up rapidly.
In that connection also let me emphasize again that there is no hope of bringing prices down voluntarily. I, and other hon. members, asked witnesses time and time again whether they wanted to bring the prices down voluntarily, and they laughed at the question instead of taking it seriously, and humorously said that they were in a system in which it was necessary for them to make good while making good was possible; that if they did not make good then, they would go to the bad at some other time, and that, therefore, they were taking all the slack in that they possibly could whenever it slackened up, so that they could take it in. That was the attitude of all the witnesses.
I want to quote next Mr. Graham F. Towers, governor of the Bank of Canada. He was questioned at pages 3361 and 3369 of the evidence as follows:
Q. Have you any suggestions to this committee how prices can be brought down by voluntary methods?
A. No, sir.
Q. That being the ease would you say there is practically no chance of prices going down throughout the world as a whole, and particularly here in Canada where of course we are most interested, as long as the world scarcity of food continues?

A. I think that is probably the case.
Mr. Thatcher:	Unless controls come back?
the Witness:	Unless prices are forced down
by controls.
At page 10 of the committee report the following appears:
The committee does not feel that the interests of Canadian consumers would be safeguarded by a system of over-all price and related controls.
Then it goes on to make a suggestion that a measure of price controls might be advisable here and there. I want to emphasize strongly my view that it is not possible to control prices effectively in spots. I think the criticism which has been made in this house and elsewhere about price controls is that you must make it comprehensive and you must have the weight, of public opinion behind you. I think that is a fair statement. I do not believe that we can effectively control prices by just having one item here and another item there under control. In that connection I want to quote again Mr. K. W. Taylor, chairman of the wartime prices and trade board, who was perhaps the most authoritative witness whom we had before the committee on matters of this kind. He said:
As I said before, efficient price control, the fixing of prices, is just the beginning of your problem; that the fixing of prices is just the first step. You have got to have a great range of controls which must buttress and support your fixed prices.
None of this is an argument against price controls in emergencies, when prolonged physical shortages of goods are inescapable.
Mr. Graham Towers had this to say under questioning:
Q. Would you need to have an over-all control?
A. Yes. If you didn't start off that way it would very soon become that.
Q. You could not apply it to just some commodities?
A. I hesitate to say you could not apply it to Yo-Yo's without going beyond that; if you see what I mean.
Q. I mean that is an extreme case? A. Yes.
Q. We are speaking now of action to reduce the general price level.
A. Then I think it would have to be an overall affair.
Why then could we not suggest over-all control at least until such time as we have got over these shortages? The answer is given again by Mr. K. W. Taylor, chairman of the wartime prices and trade board, who said:
Under the Canadian price ceiling policy the general level of retail prices, or the cost of living, was kept almost completely stable for more than four years. This was achieved by a vigorous combination of supply controls, production

Report of Prices Committee
directives, export controls, bulk purchasing, subsidies and rationing. It was a tough and realistic policy, very ably administered and firmly enforced; but its success was predicated on the whole-hearted acceptance of the policy and the procedures by practically all industries, groups, sections and classes.
That is another very fair statement that we shall have to accept, but I do not think we are right if we leap to the conclusion that there is no popular support for this today.

speechtext:
When the house rose at six o'clock I had been pointing out that the recommendations made by the committee with respect to price controls were half-hearted and that the committee proposes to deal only partly with controls. I had quoted Mr. Taylor and the prices board to the effect that price control must be a comprehensive undertaking if it is to be successful. I had also indicated that there were some people who thought that popular support, which was one of the reasons why price controls during the w'ar were so successful, could hardly be expected from people during times of peace. It is claimed today that public opinion would not support a policy of price controls sufficiently to make it work. That is an assumption.
It has been said that these controls were supported by all sections of the Canadian people during the war because of the great need for winning, and because of the danger in which the nation found itself, but that such support would not be available once the war ended. I submit, Mr. Speaker, that all the evidence is to the contrary. I believe that the people of Canada would be glad voluntarily to support a system of proper controls in peacetime as in war, provided that the same need is there and that they have a proper objective for so doing. I would support that opinion by referring to the last Gallup poll on controls a few months ago, which showed that more than seventy-five per cent of the people favoured the reimposition of controls.
I now wish to turn for a moment to high profits and their relation to prices. I do not hold the view-nor do I think any member of my group does-that high profit which may be made by any individual concern is in itself of great importance in affecting the price level. But we say that a profit system which goes all the way down the lines does have a tremendous effect on the price level. In our inquiry we have found that high profits in some instances were made by individual corporations. As a matter of fact, that

I wish to give a ruling on the amendment moved by the hon. member for Cariboo (Mr. Irvine), and seconded by the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Maclnnis). The amendment proposed for the consideration of the house is for the restoration of price controls and of the machinery necessary to make them effective. I would call the attention of the house to section 2 (a) of the amendment, which reads as follows:

This is substantially the same question that was negatived by the house when it divided on an amendment proposed by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell). Mr. Speaker, without wishing to give offence to any of the hon. gentlemen who have preceded me, I wish to say that at no time have I been adept in the art of making a hogshead of lather out of an ounce of soap; so I shall make my remarks as brief and to the point as I can, in view of the general desire to terminate this session as quickly as possible.
It was my pleasure and privilege to be a member of the prices committee, though not from its inception. I commenced my service with it at the end of April, in the position previously occupied by my colleague the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Johnston).
First I should like to endorse the compliments which have been paid by previous speakers to the chairman of the committee, the counsel and the members as a whole, but in endorsing their remarks, I must say there was a notable omission from the compliments that were extended. I believe the witnesses who appeared before the committee, representing various businesses, also deserve a compliment for the contribution they made to the work of that committee, and I wish them

Report oj Prices Committee
to know that, as a member, I certainly appreciate the information I obtained. I believe they should be complimented, not only for the information they gave and the patience with which they submitted to cross-examination, but also for the manner in which they overlooked what in some instances 1 consider were positive insults. Perhaps that language is somewhat strong, but sometimes I felt that if I had been in the place of the witness I would have been tempted to make much stronger replies to the questions asked.
I voted for the setting up of this committee in the first place; not because I felt that anything startling or unusual would be revealed, but because I felt that, information might be brought forward which would dispel some of the false impressions abroad in the country, and also that, as a result of the work of the committee, we might be better able to determine what should be done in the circumstances. I believe a good deal of information was placed on the record which, if the public could become aware of it, would dispel certain false impressions which are abroad.
As has been indicated already by the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming). I opposed the adoption of the report by the committee. Manj' of the reasons for which I felt I was justified in opposing it were advanced by the hon. member for Eglinton. In the main I believe the criticisms he offered were quite justified and I endorse most of them.
But I had an additional reason for opposing adoption of the report. I think my chief reason was the attitude adopted by the government members, which I resented very much. When I spoke on the motion to set up this committee I said I thought one reason the government was glad to take that action was that for the time being it would silence the wrath of the people with respect to the high cost of living. It would enable the government to offer the excuse that a parliamentary committee was investigating the matter, and as long as that committee sat they could transfer the responsibility from themselves to the committee. The committee has now finished its work; certain recommendations have been made, but I agree with those who have suggested that it still remains to be seen how effective those recommendations will be if carried out. Personally I consider them woefully inadequate to meet the situation.
The attitude on the part of the government members of the committee which I resented so much was expressed in the manner in which many of the witnesses who appeared before the committee were dealt with. I resented
the suggestion that, instead of being regarded as public benefactors, most of the witnesses who appeared there seemed to find the atmosphere like that of a sort of inquisition. They were looked upon as public enemies, who had to account for some wrongdoing. That was the impression I received from the manner in which many of the questions were asked; and I am going to read a few excerpts from the records of the committee to substantiate what I have said. I would not say that applied in every instance; nevertheless in many cases it was true.
Naturally I tried to discover a motive, and the only motive I could arrive at was that up to that time-and it is still the case-the government were not prepared to meet their responsibility in the way I at least think they should. The government have not met their responsibility because they have not done those things I believe they should do for the people of Canada, and therefore the government must look for a scapegoat. I considered the attitude they took toward many of these businessmen was because they were looking for a scapegoat for their own sins. They were attempting to make private business the scapegoat for their sins. In my view it was most unfair for the committee, and furthermore I believe it is a dangerous attitude to take.
From all sides of the house we have heard expressions of fear of the communist menace with its danger to the private enterprise system and freedom in general. The government, the Liberal party and the Progressive Conservative party nominally at least represent themselves as being the champions of the private enterprise system. Yet if one goes over the evidence somewhat carefully he will find that a concerted effort was made in the committee to discredit private business-or at least it had that effect. I am satisfied, from the newspaper reports which went out in consequence of some of the questions asked in committee, that many of the public are under the impression that a large number of businessmen are just a lot of bloated profiteers and chiselers. I believe there is too much of that impression abroad. There has been too much of it abroad for too long a time, without those wiho claim to be the champions of private enterprise lending any more emphasis to it.
Just to indicate a little more specifically what I mean, I should like to refer to one instance of this. While I think of it, perhaps I should say at this juncture that I can understand hon. members of the C.C.F. party doing that, because they have come out flat-footed and have said they are opposed to the private
Report oj Prices Committee

enterprise system and opposed to profit. Therefore it is in their political interest to discredit private business as much as they can so as to give them an excuse for nationalizing industry.
However I cannot understand that attitude on the part of those who pretend to be the champions of private enterprise. Therefore I resented the attitude taken by some of the Liberal members on the committee when dealing with some of these matters. The case to which I shall refer is one where possibly we cannot altogether excuse the people involved. But again, as has already been pointed out, I think the .circumstances are attributable to government policy. It was the government which was really responsible. They made possible the circumstances under which these things could happen. Then government members have the gall to turn around and blame someone for taking advantage of those circumstances.
Here is one instance of it-and in this particular instance I think the general public would get the impression that most of the fruit and vegetable business was carried on in this manner, and that profits of this kind, were made regularly in that business. This is the case of Mr. Ruben Marlow, general manager of Marlow and Company Limited of Toronto. It is the case of the famous four carloads of potatoes. I should like to indicate here the way in which this man was spoken to and in which he was treated, which I thought was unfair and uncalled for, in view of the conditions for which the government itself was responsible.
The hon. member for Victoria (Mr. May-hew) was in the chair at the time, and it is his remarks I am going to quote. This/is what he said to Mr. Marlow:
I want to say this; it is my opinion, and it is a little more than an opinion that, in this particular transaction, both the government and its departments were trying to see that there was a supply of new potatoes on the market. The foreign exchange control board released American funds for this purpose. It would appear to me you took advantage of the situation and you prevented potatoes from getting to the public at a reasonable price. In other words, you did not live up to the spirit of the regulations which existed at that time. You took an exceedingly high mark-up. I certainly will draw this to the attention of those writing the report because I think you are doing a disservice, not only to yourself and to the people of Canada, but to the other people in your own business.
Then, when I myself pressed the witness to make a comment upon that statement, the acting chairman said this further:
I fully understand the explanation you make. As far as I am concerned there is no explanar\Ir. Kuhl.]
tion at all, there is no justification for it. There is no justification in your having taken the mark-up on the potatoes which you did at that time. That is my opinion. Those who are writing the report -will have to deal with it in their own way. I feel it is my duty to make that quite plain. As I see it, I consider it one of the most outstanding cases of its kind that has yet been brought to the attention of this committee.
So far as I recall, it was shown that this particular wholesaler had made 43 per cent on the sales of two carloads of potatoes. That is undoubtedly a very high profit. He justified it himself. He considered that it was fair, in the light of prices of vegetables at that time. I considered these statements of the vicechairman a most unwarranted censure of a businessman. In any event, I think the committee could have made statements of that kind among themselves, without saying it to the man personally.

I could understand that attitude on the part of members of the C.'C.F. party, because a't all times they are attempting to show up business in the most unfavourable light possible. That, was possibly one of the strongest remarks made by the C.C.F. members on the committee, and it was quite unwarranted considering the evidence 'that was given later. Here are the words of the hon. member for Moose Jaw in addressing one of the witnesses, as reported on page 3713 of the proceedings:
Would it not look to this committee that this is one of the most shocking examples of a company not showing their strength in order to keep these prices down? There is no sense of public responsibility there because if every company in Canada took the view that you have been taking we would have uncontrolled inflation in this country andi an inevitable depression. I do not know what your justification is for that time taking such a terrific and abnormal profit.
That is typical of the questions asked and the inferences drawm by the C.C.F. members of the committee. I can, well expect that, because it is their ambition and objective to substitute nationalized industry for private industry and they will do anything they can to discredit private industry.
I should like to make one more reference to the criticisms of the hon. member for Moose Jaw. I have often said that if the truth were known members of the C.C.F., socialists and others who subscribe to a like philosophy are not as much opposed to profit as they are envious because they are not making the profits themselves. Actually I think they believe in the profit motive for themselves, and I have a little quotation which will substantiate that. This is our good friend, the hon. member for Moose Jaw, speaking to Mr. Wolfe, general manager of the Ontario Produce Company. Mr. Wolfe said:
Let me put it this way. If we were able to get the Toronto trade together to maintain a lower level on the price of our produce could we not likewise get them together to hold prices up at some time when supply and demand could bring lower prices?
Mr. Thatcher:	I am not suggesting you
should have got together, but I think possibly you could have set an example. It looks like the example you set was a bad one. You took all you could get. Maybe I would do the same thing if I were in your spot.
When C.C.F. members are off-guard they really reveal what they feel inside. As I say,
I can understand that type of criticism emanating from C.C.F. members, because they claim they' are opposed to the private enterprise system. It seems to make no difference what is discussed in this house or in the committees, the discussion always resolves itself eventually into a debate on the principles espoused by the various political parties. The questions asked in the committee were coloured by the particular philosophy subscribed to by the hon. member asking them. That is quite natural.
As I said in the beginning, innuendoes that the private enterprise system is responsible for the high cost of living should not emanate from members on the government side. They represent themselves as being the champions of private enterprise and they should so conduct themselves. There was altogether too much time taken up in the committee in an effort to blame private business for the high cost of living.
The hon. member for Cariboo (Mr. Irvine), who just preceded me, made some statement, about profits being high. I think I followed fairly closely all the evidence that was given and outside of the potato case and one or two others there were few instances where there were what one could call high profits. In most instances the profits were quite modest and in some cases there were none at all. There were times when the profits were less than they were under controls.
I should like to refer to a statement with regard to mark-up and controls by Mr. Steinberg of the Steinberg groceterias. He was being questioned by the hon. member for Moose Jaw as follows:
Q. You are telling us the retailer has not benefited particularly or has not made any greater profits with controls off than he did when they were on?
A. No, I would think the retailer has made less.
Q. Has made less?
A. Yes.
Q. Then he has not benefited by the fact controls were removed?
By Mr. Kuhl:
Q. Therefore the consumer has benefited as a consequence of the controls coming off?
A. I would say yes.

speechtext: Prices went up 25 per cent notwithstanding.

We are talking about profits, not prices. The hon. member for Cariboo stated that profits were greater, and I am just giving an instance where a retailer said his profits were less after the controls had been taken off. The hon. member for Cariboo said that profits have increased since 1939, but that is only part of the picture. As production
Report oj Prices Committee

increases, it is only natural that profits will increase correspondingly, even though the profit rate is no higher. I have not any figures before me, but I think that is the case. While profits have increased since 1939, I think it is taken for granted that the rate of profit is in conformity with that increase and is certainly no higher.
I have here another statement which I think will be of interest to the consumers of Canada. I know that when I or anyone else makes statements of this kind those who are not actuated by the best of motives may say I am trying to defend big business.
I do not want to see anyone taken advantage of, no matter who he is. The truth and the whole truth should be known about the situation. I think the general public has had the impression that tremendous profits are being made by the packing plants. I have heard that all over the country.
Here is an interesting statement in connection with the profits on meat by Mr. Millard, president and general manager of Swift Canadian Company. He was being questioned by the chairman of the committee, as follows:

question. If you take schedule 4 for 1946 and 1947 you will see that for most of those months in those two years-

I endorse wholeheartedly the suggestion made by the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming) that government policy is largely responsible for the high level of prices.
