speechtext: That is not the case.

maintopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext: It is a question of whether it is a fact or not, and the sooner the hon. gentleman recognizes some of these facts, the better it will be for him and all the rest of us. While on that point, may I say that some of our Liberal friends should be clothing themselves in sackcloth and ashes for attempting to place the blame for high prices on private business when they themselves are responsible for those high prices, and if they continue in their present course they will find that they are driving this country right into the arms of socialism and communism.

maintopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext: Why?

maintopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext:
I think I have given the hon. gentleman sufficient information on that point. By their attitude in the committee, the government members have done a great deal to discredit private business in the eyes of the public, and those who are gullible will be driven to say: If that is what private enterprise is and does, let us do away with it, and let us have instead C.C.F. and communism. There is too much of that attitude abroad already without so-called supporters of private enterprise lending any more emphasis to it. It is time that the members of the Liberal party did a little soulsearching and discovered what the real facts are which contribute to the high cost of living.
I endorse wholeheartedly the suggestions which have been made that the government do much more with respect to the taxation angle. That particular aspect interested me most in examining the witnesses. I attempted on most occasions to get a statement from the various witnesses as to the proportion of their costs represented by taxation but not many of them were very definite until on the last day we received a statement which the hon. member for Eglinton has put on the record indicating that around fourteen per cent of the cost of commodities was represented by dominion taxation.

Report of Prices Committee
I know that the opinion is held by both orthodox economists and socialists that there must be taxation. I grant that at the moment when we have well-nigh full employment a certain amount of taxation is necessary, but certainly taxation on the lower incomes could be completely eliminated. In regard to the questions I put to the witnesses, it was suggested both :by the chairman and by some of the witnesses that it was ridiculous to think of eliminating taxation. Those who hold that view hold it purely because they have not yet had their eyes opened with respect to the relationship of money to wealth. They still have much to learn.
In conclusion, I quote the last recommendation of the committee, which states:
The committee wishes to emphasize the fact that increased production at home and abroad is the only permanent solution to the problem of high prices.
I think that is one of the most important statements made by the committee. It is, of course, obvious and self-evident that increased production is the only solution, but the question which arises is, how are we to bring about that increased production? The recommendations which the government has included in this report are woefully short of any methods of stimulating production to the levels necessary to produce prices. Consequently I urge that the government members consider the taxation angle, for their own sake. There is no particular reason why I should be concerned about them personally; but, after all, we are all Canadians; we all want the highest standard of living which this country is capable of producing, and we all desire to retain our freedom. As I have already suggested, unless some appropriate action is taken in the near future to stimulate production to higher levels, and particularly to enable the people in the lower income brackets to acquire more of this production then I fear that we may be driven into the arms of totalitarianism. I think the circumstances at the moment are that serious, and therefore I urge that the members of the government consider this taxation angle seriously before it is too late.

maintopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Shortly after we reconvened here early in the year we had to deal with this question of prices and the high cost of living. Today in the closing hours of the session we are again dealing with the question of prices and the high cost of living. That is wise and proper because, of all the questions that are troubling the minds of the people of Canada today, the
most pressing is that of the high cost of living. The problem is important and impelling because it affects the people so intimately and so many of them. Perhaps seventy-five per cent of the people of Canada today find difficulty in making ends meet, in keeping their families properly fed and clothed, in keeping out of debt and that sort of thing, on account of continually rising prices.
To make ends meet has always been a struggle for the great majority of the people of every country, but since the end of the war it has been next to impossible in Canada. Since the beginning of 1946 the rise in prices has been crushing living standards like a steam-roller.
When we were discussing the setting up of the committee in February last, I said I did not consider it necessary for the government to appoint a committee to find out what was causing prices to rise. Further, I said the government had abundant information on the question. I pointed out that the same factors were operating to raise prices in 1948 as operated to raise prices in 1941. The government knew what the underlying factors were in 1941 and applied the remedy, and if they were prepared to apply the remedy, and convince the people of Canada that it was the remedy, then there was no use in having an investigation. The investigation was being instituted, I said, solely to prevent embarrassment to the government in the house.
I pointed out that the cause of rising prices was not necessarily the profiteering of private corporations or private individuals; that such profiteering where it existed was merely incidental; that the cause of rising prices was short supply and heavy effective demand. To the extent that there was profiteering, it was the inevitable consequence of the operation of the system under which we are living. There is no use in complaining about it or in thinking we will get away from it.
When the hon. member for Cariboo (Mr. Irvine) spoke this afternoon he said that in a few years from now we would likely be investigating, not high prices but low prices. We had an investigation into low prices not so very long ago. I am afraid that many hon. members have either not read the report of the price spreads commission, or, if they have read it, they have forgotten about it. In order to refresh their memories and perhaps stimulate their curiosity so that they will take a little time off and look into the report, I am going to read two or three short paragraphs from it. May I say the report was signed by five or six Conservative members
Report oj Prices Committee

who are not now members of the house and three Liberal members, only one of whom is here at the present time, namely the Minister of Justice. A report that the Minister of Justice signs is not to be thrown aside without consideration. On page 5 of the report I find the following:
The depression has, furthermore, demonstrated that the strong and the organized are attaining an ever-increasing position of dominance in our economic life; that economic power is becoming concentrated. With this concentration, old theories of economic control are proving inadequate.
If that was true in 1934, and it was, how much more true is it today because of the development and concentration of economic powers in the last fourteen years?
Then, on the next page I find this:
Fundamentally, the problems which confronted the commission are those of a transitional economy, in which simple competition still prevailed in some parts, monopoly had succeeded it in others, and monopolistic or imperfect competition characterized the rest.
That again is the situation today, as was very well indicated by the committee on cartels a few years ago, and by the evidence given by the commissioner of the Combines Investigation Act when he appeared before the prices committee. It seems to me amazing that even the hon. member for Jasper-Edson (Mr. Ku'hl) can- not be convinced by the evidence of economic exploitation that is coming to light every day.
About five or six months ago the combines investigation commissioner held an investigation into the combine in dental supplies. Broadly speaking, he found that they were making us pay through the nose for our false teeth. And the evidence brought out by the prices committee showed that when we had paid for these teeth the price of food went up so high that we did not have anything to chew. Just a few weeks ago we had another report from the commissioner, this time on eyeglasses. Surely to goodness we should awake to the fact that these things do not arise from the innate depravity of human beings. They arise because of the competitive struggle of making an existence, as the committee of 1934 said in its report on page 7:
It is the fierceness of the struggle, not any unusual depravity in the men concerned, which leads to the adoption of such practices. No one businessman can afford to follow the dictates of his conscience and refuse to conform. If he did, he would be eliminated.
In the economic world in which we are living today, to be eliminated in the struggle for existence is not a thing to contemplate with any degree of complacency. Tomorrow most

hon. members will go to church and will hear sermons on the golden rule, to do unto others as you would have them do unto you. But on Monday morning we have another golden rule-there is one for Sunday and another for the resit of the week'-which is, "Do others before they do you." That is the system under which we are living, and that is why we have the conditions which are complained of ait the present time. I am not complaining about people doing things that circumstances compel them to do in order to survive in (the business world. My complaint is that the representatives of the people should allow such things to be done.
The committee's report is, to say the least, disappointing. In one of the paragraphs in the conclusion, I believe it is stated that the mere fact that the committee was sitting, if it did not prevent prices from rising, at least prevented them from going up as much as they might have done if the committee bad not been sitting at all. Perhaps that is true. Perhaps the words of Longfellow-
(Nothing useless is, or low;
Each thing in its place is best.
-would apply in this instance, and perhaps some good was done. But when you come to the cost of living index and see how it has gone up since this committee was organized, you will see that the committee has not done so much after all. At page 14 of the report I find this:
In 1946, prices began to rise more quickly and then accelerated rapidly under the pressure of factors that are examined. By April of 1948, the index had risen to 151-6. while on the first of January, 1946, it stood at 119-9. This was an increase of 26 per cent or twice the increase which had occurred during the war years.
Hon. members will note that the paragraph begins by saying that in 1946 prices began to rise rapidly and became accelerated under the pressure of the factors that they were investigating. As a matter of fact, prices went up in every instance as soon as controls were removed. I am not saying it would be an easy matter to maintain controls. My hon. friends to my right must accept a large share of the blame-and there is no use in their blaming the government-for the removal of these controls by the government. They are both competing for the favour of the same people; and the government undoubtedly was afraid that if they did not remove controls, the official opposition might make capital out of that fact.
The report gives only the index figures for April. The cost of living index for May is still higher. I do not know why it was not given here. In May it was up to 153-3. That

Report of Prices Committee
is a rise of 33-4 points since January 1, 1946. When we come to food, the index is up a great deal more. In January 1, 1946, it stood at 132-8; in May, 1948, it stood at 191-2; or, in other words, it was up in that period of about seventeen months by 58-4 points, or almost 44 per cent.
Did hon. members ever contemplate or ever try to analyse the way in which this rising cost of living affects the various sections of the community? For those in the upper and middle income brackets it is not particularly important. They do either one of two things: they save less, or they buy fewer luxuries. Their standard of living does not suffer. But when j'ou come down to the lower income brackets, and that includes at least sixty-five per cent or seventy-five per cent of the people of Canada, the situation is different. Among that number there are a relatively small number who can, through economic pressure, do something to raise their income as the cost of living goes up. But the great mass-that is, the unorganized worker, the small farmer, the small businessman, the person on superannuation, the person on a small pension such as old age pensioners and the like-cannot do anything to raise their income, and they get the full force and effect of the rising cost of living.
When this matter was discussed in the prices committee-I was not there at the time, having left the committee to go to another one-Mr. J. S. McLean, president of Canada Packers, said, in reference to rising prices, as reported at page 2201 of the evidence and proceedings:
When prices get too high people stop buying. Now, in so far as it is an exemplification of that, it is not only desirable, it is inevitable. When housewives make up their minds they can't afford to buy any food at the current price they stop buying.
When housewives decide that they cannot buy food, they do something else besides stopping to buy food. They get mad. The housewives of Canada today are mad-

maintopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext: At whom?

maintopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext: I will leave that for my hon. friend to answer.

maintopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext: What is your answer?

maintopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext: They find that they cannot buy the food, the clothing and the other things their families need.

maintopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext: Whom do they blame?

maintopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext:
They blame the government and perhaps their blame is well placed. I believe they blame my hon. friends to the
right, too, considering the results of recent elections. However, it is not necessary to go into that now; we can go into it at some other time. Perhaps anything we might say would be only a guess anyway. The fact of the matter is that, as the supply of goods on the consumer market is increasing, prices are not going down but are going up. If you looked for a suit of clothes two years ago every suit you saw in a store window bore the words "with priority only". You could not buy a shirt or a pair of pyjamas or a score of things now in plentiful supply in the stores; but in 1616 prices were lower than they are today. I direct attention to what the dominion bureau of statistics has to say on this matter, and I should like hon. members to understand that this situation is dangerous. It is the prelude to a depression; and you cannot just leave it alone unless you are convinced the government can do nothing; that we are the playthings of fate; that when a depression comes you take it and that when war brings a boom you take that also. Surely no self-respecting people should take an attitude like that. I have before me the Canadian Statistical Review for April, 1948, issued by the dominion bureau of statistics. The portion preceding what I am about to read contained a summary of the improvement in production and referred to the government surplus and things of that kind. Then it went on to say:
In contrast to the strength shown by data on production and employment there has been some evidence that the volume of goods moving through retail channels is smaller than it was a year ago. Retail sales during the first quarter of 1!M8 were up only 11-4 per cent over the first quarter of 1947. even though Easter sales fell entirely in March this year. But the index of retail commodity prices was up almost double this amount, about 22- per cent, an indication that the physical volume of goods sold is dorvn.
The evidence is that, as our ability to produce goods increases, the ability of the people to buy and consume those goods decreases. Some hon. members may remember that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) referred to this matter in his budget speech. In this debate I suppose I am not allowed to quote him; but he pointed out that, people were using up not only their current income but also the savings they accumulated during the war. It is even worse than that. They are not only consuming all their current income; they have not only consumed their savings; but they are now- buying on credit, paying in instalments, and that cannot continue for very long. When they have reached their limit in instalment buying they will have only their current income, less what is required to pay the instalment purchases, and then sales will
Report of Prices Committee

decline faster than they declined in the period referred to by the bureau of statistics.
This is the situation facing the country. Surely we should be able to do something about it, but in my opinion there is nothing in the report of the committee that will help in a material way to remedy this situation.
Before resuming my seat, since I do not want to prolong this debate unduly, I should like to refer to just one other matter. As I said earlier, the committee was appointed in order to avoid embarrassment to the government. The report is made in order to avoid the same embarrassment; and the inquiry recommended is intended to keep people quiet, in the hope that something will happen between now and when the house meets next winter. One of the very few submissions made to the committee by organizations came from the Canadian association of consumers. The brief was read and spoken to by the president, Mrs. R. J. Marshall, and the secretary. Mrs. F. E. Wright. In my opinion they presented an excellent brief, for which they are to be highly commended. They gave some information as to the effect of high prices on family life. What I am about to read appears on pages 1076 and 1077 of the minutes of proceedings and evidence of the committee. They refer to a study of the effect of the increased cost of living on family life, made by the Hamilton family service bureau in November and December, 1947. This survey covered seventy families, averaging 5-8 persons, with an average income in 1947 of SI,820. The survey showed that most families spent from 24 to 39 per cent of their income, or amounts ranging from S24 to S45 a month per family for food in 1939, but that in 1947 they had to spend from 40 to 80 per cent of their income, or from S50 to $100 a month to buy the same quantity of food. The wages of ordinary workers have not gone up by anything like that amount. Then they say:
These surveys and widespread reports which we have had from consumers lead us to believe:
(a)	Family living costs have increased to a much greater extent than wages and family income;
(b)	The standard of living is being lowered;
(c)	Many families are reducing the quantities of their food purchases below an adequacy for nutritional health;
(d)	Excessively high prices, particularly of essential commodities, are likely to result in many families exhausting their savings, going into debt or over-extending themselves in instalment buying.
That is exactly what I have said is already being done. That statement is supported, not only by the evidence brought forward in this brief, but by reports coming from various parts of Canada and also the United States.

I suggest to the government that it should do more than what is contained in this milk and water report-more water than milk. Something more is required. But before we leave here, and after this report is endorsed-and I suppose we have to endorse it, because it is the best we can get-we should have some assurance from the government that it will pay some attention to the report; because, unless we have that assurance, we are not doing anything to ease the misery of the people, and to stave off the catastrophe which will overtake us unless we change our methods.

maintopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, since the amendment moved by the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming) has been ruled out of order, and since the amendment moved by the hon. member for Cariboo (Mr. Irvine) met the same fate, what is before the house at the present is a motion for concurrence in the report of the prices committee. Since I do not think any members of the official opposition have yet spoken directly to that report, but rather have discussed our own amendment, I should like to say at the outset that we are totally unable to accept the report, and that we find it a mere vague collection of words designed, as has been said and has been proven, to divert the attention of the people, and particularly of the housewives, from the object of what should be their real censure, namely the government's policies in their effect on prices; and to try to divert some of their attention, to prices outside Canada-anywhere but where it should be directed, and that is on the shoulders of the government.
It is for this reason mainly that we cannot support the report or vote for its adoption. The hon. member for Eglinton, in his extremely able and telling speech of this afternoon, has analysed most of the deficiencies in the report. Its conclusions are wrong. The committee has not served its purpose, because it did not report on the real causes of the increases isn prices. It did not actually say what the actual evidence proves, and indeed whaJt some parts of its own report lead to as the only obvious conclusion, namely, that the government's policies almost exclusively have been responsible for the increased cost of living in Canada.
Speeches of hon. members in the C.C.F. patty in this debate have imported a certain air of unrealism. They have introduced into the debate the theory of over-all controls and the theory of a planned economy as against the free enterprise system. In their usual fashion they have sought to leave the impression that anyone who takes part in free enter-

Report of Prices Committee
prise is out to do his neighbour-in fact that was the statement of the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Maclnnis). He stated that the philosophy of the free enterprise system is "to do others before they do you."
They are welcome to that point of view. It indicates the unreal world in which they live. The fact that they have that point of view, and put it forward with obvious sincerity, makes it impossible to believe that they are putting it forward merely for political purposes. It is impossible to 'believe that that is their only reason. It is certainly one of their reasons; but if that were the only reason one might say, "Well, at least they ore realists so far as their own interests are concerned; at least they are trying to get into power by painting a picture which they know to be untrue." But unfortunately-or perhaps fortunately-that is not 'the whole situation. I am beginning to think they really do believe it.

maintopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext: Oh. they can't be that stupid! I don't believe that!

maintopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext:
It would appear that the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Gibson) gives them credit for even greater subtlety than I do. However I am glad to have the reassurance he gives me, because I was beginning to think that the C.C.F. really thought that what they say about free enterprise is actually true. I am glad to know they do not, and I am glad also to have the confirmation of an independent member, free from political bias.
In any event, that is what they say they believe about the free enterprise system, that it has a social philosophy based upon the principle of doing others before they do you. In any event, that is the basis of their approach to this whole situation. Consequently they have introduced a note of unreality into the debate.
Let me sav, before going on, that there is one part of their argument which should be answered clearly and in such a way as to leave no doubt in the minds of hon. members, the C.C.F. party, or the people of Canada, and that is for me to say that they are not the only party which has at heart the welfare of the average man and woman in Canada. That, of course, is the impression they have been seeking to leave in the country for many years.

maintopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext: That is scarcely peculiar to the C.C.F.

maintopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext:
It is with a spirit of selfrighteousness that they have introduced into this debate the suggestion that they are the only ones who have at heart the interests of 5849-378
the common people of Canada. That, of course, is not a fact. The fact is that I believe everyone in the House of Commons, every party in the country, has at heart the interests of the people of Canada. We criticize the government, yes; we say their policies are not working in the best interests of the people of Canada. But we do not say they are doing this deliberately. The only people who say that about the government, about the official opposition and about anyone else who disagrees with them, is the C.C.F. That, I suggest, proves clearly again the world of unreality in which they live.
It is not possible to look into people's minds and to know what goes on in those minds. But I would tell my hon. friends that I do not think those tactics work with the people. I tell my hon. friends that this party certainly has at heart the interests of every man and woman in Canada as much as they have. Indeed I believe it could be said that, we have more at heart the interests of the people in Canada, because rve do not live in that unreal world in which my hon. friends the socialists live.
We do not want to introduce into this debate or into the debate on every problem which comes up in the House of Commons this theoretical question of the substitution of a planned economy for our present system. We do not want to conduct our debates on that basis, because we prefer to advocate things which can be and should be done now to relieve the Canadian people from the increasing burden of the cost of living in Canada today. That is where our approach to the matter is a great deal more realistic than theirs because, as the hon. member for Eglinton said this afternoon, we have suggested and will continue to suggest things which should be and can be done to relieve that burden and to check the increasing cost of living.
Before I proceed further to analyse the things which should be done, I should like to deal with some of the points raised by hon. members of the C.C.F. who have taken part in the debate this evening. In the amendment moved by the hon. member for Cariboo, there was a great similarity to certain recommendations in the report of the prices committee, and particularly in the first paragraph of the amendment where there is a recommendation for the reimposition of the excess profits tax and a reversal to a policy of subsidies. Those are the recommendations contained in paragraphs 5 and 8 of the recommendations of the prices committee. It shows how closely the minds of the government-those who drew up the report anyway-and the C.C.F. run
Report oj Prices Committee

together on this and other related matters. We find the C.C.F. party strongly criticizing the report and some of its recommendations; yet we find here, as in so many other matters, they are at one as to the solution which should be adopted. They are also similar in this respect, that in the same way in which the government has failed to find or put forward a solution of the problem, I am sure that the recommendations of the C.C.F. would have equally little chance of success.
One fact emerges from the remarks of the hon. member for Cariboo and the hon. member for Vancouver East, namely, that the CjC.F. solution of this problem is in a reversal to a system of over-all price control. The hon. member for Cariboo devoted almost all his remarks to that idea. He quoted certain evidence given before the committee by Mr. K. W. Taylor, president of the wartime prices and trade board. The whole tenor of the portions of the evidence which the hon. member quoted was to the effect that, under the present stresses and strains, the free enterprise system would result in a certain upward pressure on prices. The hon. member quoted with approval those portions of the remarks of the chairman of the wartime prices and trade board, and he referred to him as being a highly qualified witness in this and other related matters.
That being the case, I am sure the hon. member will give equal credence to other passages of the evidence of the same witness, because those passages are important in connection with this particular matter. In the early stages of the committee meetings, Mr. Taylor was discussing the question of the reversion to over-all price control, the very matter the hon. member for Cariboo was discussing this afternoon. The relevant portion of the witness' remarks in that particular connection is to be found on page 61 of the minutes of proceedings and evidence of the committee. Mr. Taylor saidi this:
A "free economy" is predominantly based upon and organized by a system of free prices- free, .that is, within the general framework of the law. In a free economy, prices constitute the main guide to production, and are at the same time the balance-wheel of supply and demand. Rising prices for one commodity indicate relative shortage and invite both increased production and economy in consumption; falling prices, in turn, indicate relative surplus and produce a tendency to ease up on production and to increase consumption. In other words, it is this constant flexibility of prices that helps to keep production and consumption in reasonable balance and harmony.
I do not think even the hon. member for Cariboo in any of his remarks this afternoon disagreed with that portion of Mr. Taylor's

evidence. The witness went on to say this with respect to an over-all system of price control;
If a community embarks upon a system of fixed or administered prices, it must invent some substitute for the flexible price system as a means of finding out what people really want, and what they want more of, and what they want less of. Failing such a substitute, the principle of freedom tends to disappear, and the government has to decide what, will be produced and in what quantities. The free price system has many imperfections, but there has not yet been developed any other system that will preserve in essence what I call a "free economy."
Administered or government-determined prices inevitably entail considerable government control over the details of production and distribution. And the wider the range, and the longer the duration of administered prices the more detailed must these controls become.
I think I should emphasize, out of a considerable background of experience, that the fixing of a price is only the beginning of price control. During the war years we found that the making of actual price decisions was not too difficult, and formed only a minor part of our work. It was the efforts to assure supply, to estimate what was needed, to see that things were fairly (! istribated, to protect the consumer against upgrading or degradation of quality, it was the interminable investigating, checking and blocking of loop-holes for evasion that made up by far the larger part of each month's work.
None of this is an argument against price controls in emergencies, when prolonged physical shortages of goods are inescapable. But I do suggest that these considerations should be carefully weighed whenever any broad extension of continuing government price fixing is proposed.
We have already heard of how in another portion of his remarks the chairman of the wartime prices and trade .board spoke of the chaos that would result from a roll-back and the imposition of over-all controls. Those two portions of his evidence go together. The portion with which I am concerned and the point I want to make here is that the chairman of the wartime prices and trade board admits that if you start control you have to go the whole way. You cannot have partial control and partial freedom in our economy.
The hon. member for 'Cariboo dealt with another portion of Mr. Taylor's statement in his remarks this afternoon, when he admitted that shortages exist. In fact I think he went so far as to admit that shortages are the main cause of the present increases in prices under the present system. I suggest that if he believes that he will agree that at present there is only one solution consistent with the maintenance of our free system, and that is increased production. Greater production, greater abundance is the solution. That is the main solution, the main requirements for a restoration of

Report of Prices Committee
balance in our economy and for lower prices. And in order to achieve more production we need, not more taxation but less taxation. That is the inconsistency in the hon. gentleman's proposal which he made this afternoon, because there he advocated more taxation.
1 think the hon. gentleman's party, that is, the C.C.F.. as a whole agrees with the position he took this afternoon when he said it was not possible to control prices in spots. We all agree with that. If he will admit that it is impossible to control prices only in spots, why will he not take the other logical step and admit that it is not possible to control our economy only in spots, that you cannot have control of prices unless you have control over all the costs entering into production. There must then be control of raw materials, wages, prices of farm products; control of the whole economy.
Based upon the remarks of the chairman of the wartime .prices and trade board, that conclusion is inescapable. As he said, if you remove the incentive from the price system you have to substitute something in its place. Under the system of our hon. friends the socialists, that substitute would be compulsion. If you stop the working of the free enterprise system you must use force, or you will have complete stagnation. Take away the incentive to production and you will not get production. Therefore you will have to resort to something else, and the only possible thing you can resort to is force

it is force or famine. Compulsion is what it comes to under their system.
Take the case of butter. There you have a prime example of what we have been talking about. Price control of butter was re-introduced last January. I want to refer to some of the discussion which took place in this house recently. I do not agree with the hon. member for Middlesex West (Mr. McCubbin), the parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner), when he says we need not be concerned about a butter shortage next fall. I think we shall probably have one. If you compare the export figures of dairy cattle to the United States this year and last you will find that exports are running about double last year's volume. I have here the latest Department of Agriculture Live Stock Market Review of June 24. and on the first page it gives the exports of dairy cattle to the south, totalling for the week 4,761 head, making a total to date this year of 46,417. greater this year than last, and the figures for the year to date are twice as high this year as last. The logical conclusion of the solution advocated by the C.C.F., namely, the restoration of over-all controls in peacetime, is the use of force to secure production. That can be made as a statement of fact, because we can see in the words of C.C.F. speakers, themselves, that that is what they want. We know, from listening to their remarks in this country, that is what they want and what they are prepared to contemplate. To substantiate the statement I have made, I remind the house that the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis), when speaking on the labour estimates on June 24, said we would have to revert eventually in this country to a system of directed labour. His words can be found at page 5822 of Hansard. That was the system he wanted. That is the system they contemplate and would like to see in effect in this country-control of prices, direction of labour, the complete abolition of freedom. We surely can accept their own words for that. They are not in power in this country; but let us look at what is happening in the United Kingdom. There they have just that. They have to have it. I do not think the majority of the people there want it; I do not know if even the labour government wanted to bring it in; but in order to implement their plan, they had to have it- and they have it-control of prices and compulsion of labour. Incidentally, Mr. Speaker, a fact which my socialist friends of the C.C.F. overlook when they talk about controls is that the price level in the United Kingdom, where they have complete controls, has risen more rapidly and to a higher level than the price level in Canada or in the United States.
This is what the system of controls imposed in wartime and maintained in peacetime has done to the wholesale price level in the United Kingdom. I am quoting from the Statistical Summary of the Bank of Canada for April, 1948. In 1937 the wholesale price level in the United Kingdom stood at 109-5, and it rose by 1945 to 170-2. By March, 1948, it had risen to 218-7, or a rise between 1937 and March, 1948, of 109-2 points.

at approximately the same level as in the United Kingdom, 109-7 in Canada as against 109-5 in the United Kingdom. So there you can see what happens when you get the facts and figures under a controlled economy-control of prices, control of farm products, control of what people shall produce and when and where, and direction of labour; compulsion right across the board- and with all that you have a higher price level and a greater increase in the price level than you have in the United States, where you have free enterprise, and greater than in Canada where we are beginning to get back to free enterprise and where we have relatively a measure of abundance and could have more if the government would do those things we advocate that it should do.
Coming to the report itself, I find many reasons why one cannot concur in it. Not only does it fail, as I said at the outset, to attribute the real reasons for the increase in prices in Canada, but it contains a number of inaccuracies. On page 5, for instance under the heading of "Summary of Findings", the report says:
The committee is convinced that its action in conducting spot examinations in those commodities that are particularly vulnerable to price increases at the present time has had a deterrent effect on individuals and firms engaged in processing, handling or selling these and related commodities.
I wonder whether the committee is really convinced; I wonder whether the people who drew up this report are convinced, which I doubt. While they may be convinced that what they say is correct, the outstanding fact in the minds of the people of Canada is that the longer the prices committee has sat, the higher prices have gone. So I say there is no ground whatsoever in fact for the statement made there, and no ground for the drafters of the report to have that conviction lto which they refer.
On page 48 of the report I find a substantial error in the compiling of the figures. This is perhaps a relatively small matter, but I think it should be set right immediately, because it gives am entirely wrong impression of what the committee found. A comparison is given of the gross profits earned by some firms

in the fruit and vegetable industry, covering five months from November to March in 194647 and 1947-48. In the first column the total in dollars is given as $80,904; in the second column, $165,539. Therefore the committee feels it is justified in saying that the net operating profit more than doubled. If you will add up the figures in the first column you will find that there is an error of $30,000 in addition. The total is just all wrong. The total should be $110,188, which means that the profits in the second period were a great deal less than double the total in the first period. Actually when one analyses it further he finds that the error is that they failed to show that one of the figures in the first column was an operating loss of $29,284 wdiioh, when subtracted from the total, leaves -the total of the first column of figures correct, but gives an entirely erroneous impression. It fails to show that the profit system is what we have always said it is, namely, not only a profit system but a profit and loss system; but the assumption which the committee makes, based on that -as to the reason for the increase in the cost of living, is entirely erroneous, and gives a wrong impression about how business is carried on. I think the chairman should see to it that the report is corrected in that particular and that any harm done is remedied.
I think what was said this afternoon by the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming) and by the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard (Mr. Merritt) sufficiently analysed the main weaknesses in this report and sufficiently showed the true situation and the true cause of the rise in prices. Therefore I will not attempt to duplicate the presentations which they have made; but in summary form I do want to indicate, first, wherein government policies have been responsible for the increase and what steps we would take, what steps we urge the government to take, to meet the situation and to relieve -the people of Canada of the increase and to get living costs down again.
First, rising prices have come about because of shortages in essential commodities. That initial shortage situation can hardly be blamed on the government. It was caused by the war. But it. was aggravated by our decision, properly taken and agreed to by all, to extend relief and rehabilitation to the United Kingdom and to Europe. The point I make there is that the government knew about that shortage. It knew that its program of relief and rehabilitation would aggravate these shortages, yet it took no adequate steps to ensure that our production of these essential commodities would be increased to meet those commitments which we have to fulfil.

The second cause of increase in prices is, of course, inflation, increase of the amount of money in circulation in proportion to the goods available for sale. In that connection the government's policies are directly responsible for the increase in the cost of living. As an illustration of what I have in mind, I want to refer to the last budget. Although we had a surplus of $700 million as a result of high taxation, we were told that if we left the money in the taxpayers' pockets we would increase inflation. We were told that they did not know how to spend their own money, and that the government would have to spend it for them. We were told that it will be spent on debt reduction. Therefore, instead of being a taxpayer's budget, instead of being a people's budget, it became a bondholder's budget; that is all. What is the difference? If you retire bonds and put $100 for that bond back into circulation, back into the taxpayer's pocket, he has it to take out and spend. Therefore you are not preventing inflation, because just, as much money is going back into circulation. But instead of the taxpayer having more of his income in his pocket and getting relief in that way, by a lowering of the tax rates, now he has to take this little capital, which he saved before, and spend it to meet the increase in the cost of living.
The third reason is, of course, the embargoes on imports from the United States, which immediately created a series of serious shortages in Canada and set the stage for speculation. The government, having invited speculation, now seeks to pass all the blame for the situation off on to the comparatively few who indulged in speculation.
The fourth is the procedure with relation to food prices. We remember what happened last November when, well in advance, the government announced that contracts with the United Kingdom were to be re-negotiated at increased prices. Food prices immediately went up in anticipation of that re-negotiation. The same thing is happening now with relation to the price of beef. In an effort to win the election in Saskatchewan the Minister of Agriculture has been forecasting for a month the lifting of the embargo against the export of beef cattle. What could happen as a result? What the government invited happened. The farmers have held off their beef in anticipation of the lifting of the embargo, with two results: first, a growing shortage of beef on the market, and second, an increase in the price of that which remained. That is another instance of a direct, almost a deliberate, invitation to a price rise. And yet the embargo has not been removed.
Finally, we have the excise taxes which increased by 25 per cent the cost of many commodities basic in our cost of living.

These taxes, which have done more than anything else in recent years to increase the cost of living are, we hope, to be removed in the near future. Certainly the committee's report recommends it.
I wish the government would not be so sensitive to the criticism of its own members because, from authoritative statements reported in the press, one understands that, had this criticism not been made, the government might have already removed some of those taxes. One can only hope that either the government will become a little less sensitive to criticism by its own members, or that its own members will develop a better sense of timing in their approaches to the government.
In conclusion, I should like to list briefly the five measures that we would put into effect, and which should be put into effect now, to deal with the situation. First, we should free the dollar to encourage imports and thus relieve shortages and give increased production. Second, we should remove the embargoes which keep out the goods we require, thus cutting down the shortages. Third, we should remove the 25 per cent excise tax, and the sales tax from basic commodities, thus reducing the price of many essentials. Fourth, we should lower taxes and increase exemptions, thus leaving people more money in the lower income brackets, and family groups more money in their pockets to meet the increased costs, and leave more money free for investment and expansion. Fifth, we should immediately institute a large-scale natural resources development program to produce more at home and to increase the wealth and prosperity of this country.

The hon. member for Eglinton, however, who has declaimed so vigorously this afternoon about the reduction of the tax, and how it should have been reduced long 5849-379
ago-in fact, reduced before it was ever put on -did vote against it. He voted against the proposition that consideration should be given to the practicability of cutting out that tax now. Despite all his oratory this afternoon, the facts are that he voted against that recommendation; and he voted against every other recommendation, too. I suppose it would be trite to observe that actions speak louder than words. But it is true, is it not?

maintopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext: You voted both ways on that.

maintopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext: No; that was Hackett.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext: I wish also to call this to the attention of the house: the hon. member for Eglinton, and others, have inveighed against what they have called the incompleteness of the report, and have inveighed against what they call its too great voluminousness. I wish to remind them and to tell the house that there is no record of any proposal of any kind by them as to what evidence should be reviewed, as to what recommendations might be made or as to what recommendations might not be made. There just is not any positive contribution on the part of those gentlemen to be found in the records at any stage of the consideration of this report. And it is not as though they had not apparently been giving thought to it because, as a matter of fact, they were continually talking about stopping the committee work and making an interim report about something or another.

maintopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext: Will the hon. member permit a question?

maintopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext: Sit down.

maintopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext: Is it not a fact that the hon. member, while chairman of the committee, told me that if I had any suggestions to make I was to put them into the form of a motion and he would have them voted down? Will the hon. member tell me whether it was worthwhile to put forward any recommendation after his statement?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext:
This last speech hardly requires any reply. The hon. member seems to complain that he was admonished-not once; he is quite right about that, but many times- to put proposals into the form of a motion. Over and over and over again they were admonished, exhorted, urged to do something. But they could not do anything except captiously to criticize. Why should he, a parliamentarian, object when he was requested to put a proposition into the form of a motion? Why should he object to that? Is that not a proper thing to do? And from what he now says, the house will recognize the truth of what I am
Report of Prices Committee

saying, that there was no contribution at any time by any of those members in the committee. They were trying captiously to criticize and, if possible, to hold back; and if that statement is not true, they acted as if it were true.

maintopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext: You have not answered my question yet.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of National Revenue
maintopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext: It is not unusual for them.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext:
No, as the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Reid) points out, it is not. It is not unusual to have such an attitude as that from them.
Some consideration has been given to the pages of this report. It has not been pointed out that, in the main, the report is a digest of evidence. That is what takes up most of the large volume we have before us. No one has suggested that it is an unfair digest of the evidence. I think such a digest of evidence is bound to be inadequate. I feel that when you have so great a volume of evidence to review you are almost certain to do an inadequate job of pressing that into a relatively small number of pages.
At any rate, however, the best that could be done was done; and I conceive that it is a very good job, although I feel there must be some inaccuracies. I consider that it must be inadequate in some respects; but, all things considered, I believe it is a fair digest. It is never consciously unfair, and there is no singling out of evidence one way to the detriment of a case which might have been presented the other wTay.
Let me call to the attention of the house the fact that those hon. members who have criticized the report never made any reference to the fact that the evidence was presented there in digest form to the house. As a matter of fact, they talked as though they did not want the house to know it. It is there for any person to read and determine whether, in that light, the conclusions are reasonable.
The conclusions and recommendations are not put forth dogmatically. Everyone, except the hon. members who offer no assistance, admits that the problem of high prices is a most difficult one. In general that problem in Canada has been seriously affected by external prices. I do not know whether they would deny that, but they probably will. Take zinc for example, which is exported in part. The high price of that commodity in Canada is bound to be affected by what is obtainable for it in the foreign markets. So with hundreds and hundreds of the articles which we have for sale in Canada; they are affected by export prices.

So far as import prices are concerned, it is also patent that we are buying in markets where prices are high and that high-priced articles enter into production .in this country and are bound to affect prices here. But my hon. friends do not wish to admit that; they do not wish to say anything about that, and they do not wish to let anybody else say anything about it either.
That is the reason for this dissertation before the evidence is digested. That is the reason for these conclusions being arrived at. I ask that some of the conclusions be looked at shortly. In effect the first one says it probably would be good business to have continued the scrutiny of prices. That is all it says, that it probably would be of value. The hon. member for Eglinton voted against that.
It is suggested there as well as elsewhere- the hon. member took exception to this- that there is some reason for thinking that the committee sittings had had a salutary effect upon the price structure or the price level. I must admit that that is an imponderable; you cannot be sure that that is so. However, the capable women who came before the committee representing the Canadian association of consumers, a large association of keen-eyed students, asserted that they believed such to be the case. One large manufacturer stated recently that if it were not for the sittings here he would raise his prices, that he would raise them as soon as the committee rose. He was cross-examined at some length to make sure that he had not been misheard, but he was positive about it. I happen to recall it quite definitely. There were other statements of the same sort.
The hon. member for Eglinton went on to say that you should not make too much out of that. I subscribe to the idea that one swallow does not make a summer, but I think there is some reason for believing -that if there is a continued possibility of your being called up 'before an organization to explain why you are doing certain things, there will be salutary results. As I say, the hon. member for Eglinton voted against that. I do not know whether the hon. member for Vancouver-iBurrard did or not.

maintopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext: Do not worry; I would have voted against it.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext:
The second recommendation is in connection with an important arm in the administration of the government, namely, the combines investigation commission. We feel that it would be well to strengthen that. Surely there cannot be any objection to that. Surely every person here

Report, of Prices Committee
who is interested in doing what can be done to keep down prices, to see that prices are not fixed improperly, would be in favour of that. But, as I say, they are against that.
Then I come to the word "profiteer." The third recommendation is that flagrant cases of profiteering should be prosecuted. The hon. member is against that; the Tories are against that. It might very well be that the law under which such prosecution would take place might be strengthened. I think it should be. I feel that it would be much easier to discharge duties under a brief for the defence than under a brief for the prosecution, with the law as it is. Without attempting anything in the nature of iperse-cution, I think good purposes would be served by making that law stronger in order to hit out at plainly flagrant cases of profiteering.
During his speech the hon. member said that we have been indefinite in our report, that we have said that certain people seem to have done so-and-so and that something else had happened, that nobody has been named. Surely that was the fair way to report. What would he have said if this committee had asserted that John Doe was guilty of an offence? What would he have said if the committee in an ex parte examination of the matter decided that certain people were guilty and should be prosecuted?

maintopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext: You preferred a general smear.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext:
That is the sort of thing he would like this committee to do but he did not have the temerity to make a motion to that effect, although today he says this committee should have reported that certain people were guilty. The evidence was not sufficient for that and the committee wanted to be fair. It is now that the hon. member discloses himself as desiring to be unfair, although I am quite sure he will be the first one to deny that he has any such intention.
I observe that you are becoming rather restive, Mr. Speaker, because it would seem that I have come to the end of my forty minutes. I would suggest that I be allowed to continue for a minute or two, more particularly since I have been interrupted a few times. But if there should be any person who desires not to grant that to me, naturally I shall be content, because the house has been most patient in listening to me thus far.

maintopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext: Go ahead.

maintopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Has the hon. member
unanimous consent to proceed?

maintopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext: Yes'.

maintopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Not past eleven
o'clock.

maintopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext: We get Charlie McCarthy tomorrow night.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext:
I am quite sure the hon. member will be much better entertained. Of course I would not suggest that that probably is the proper mental level for him.
The next paragraph requires no particular comment. The committee felt that if it was possible, having conserved the United States dollars necessary for the time being, to get away from these bothersome and nuisancelike importation controls on fresh vegetables and fruits, that should be done. Of course the committee has to make a recommendation of that sort with some care. We must consider the labour which the people of Canada have put into the business of producing these vegetables. My own thought is that to remove prohibitions of that sort at the present time when the farmer's labour is done would not be the right and fair thing to do. It is worded deliberately in a careful manner because there are both consumers and producers to take into consideration.
I pass over with only a word the recommendation with reference to the taxing of profits. Again every person must agree that that is a difficult sort of law to work out. But if improper profits are being made, if profits rise so high that they are clearly beyond what is reasonable, then indeed it does not seem unfair to tax them, because that is where the wealth is. That is a carefully worded section. There is no general attack on business in it.
As to the remaining subjects respecting accounting and inventory reserves, I would point out that many companies, by declaring inventory reserves, have hidden, both from their shareholders and from those who work for them and from the general public, some of the wealth they have made. With many that is not so. It was shown that one company instituted a reserve policy and followed it automatically through all the years. But with other companies one could not tell without considerable search what their profits were, and it does not seem to me that there should be any objection to a complete revelation of what their profits are. Remember this, that these companies operate by virtue of a charter which has been granted to them by the legislature, and they are given a limited liability. There should not be anything objectionable in requiring a full disclosure, because they are selling their goods to the public as a whole; they are dealing with citizens of the country as labour, and they are selling their securities on the market

by virtue of the sort of annual financial statement they make. Surely, then, it is not unreasonable, when we have granted a limited liability to that kind of artificial person, to require them to disclose what the truth is respecting their business.
I could go on and speak of each one of the recommendations which have been made, but I shall not take up the time of the house to do so at any greater length. As usual, I wish to say I am grateful to hon. members for having listened to me and for having given me extra time to finish up on one or two subjects on which I wanted to speak.

maintopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker-

maintopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext: Before my hon. friend speaks, I should like to ascertain the wishes of the house about sitting after eleven o'clock.

maintopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext: No.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext: That settles it.

maintopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext: The address to which we have just listened indicates beyond words the close relationship which those on the government side of the house bear to those in the socialist party, for you will notice, Mr. Speaker, that not one word of criticism passed the lips of my hon. friend in regard to those sitting to our left.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext: He did not have time.

maintopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Here is a most interesting situation. On this which was supposed to be the last day of the session, a motion was made by my hon. friend the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin) in his dual capacity as minister and as chairman of this committee, and pot one word passed his lips. For the first time in this house, on a motion as important as this, the chairman of a committee saw fit to throw the report into the house, say nothing about the attitude of the government with regard to it, and allow a discussion, on a matter as important as this, to continue all day without any suggestion on the part of any minister of the crown as to what the government intends to do with regard to this problem.
It is most interesting to discuss, even in the few minutes at my disposal, the series of events which impelled the committee, without power to report-indeed the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) himself said that this committee should not have that power, because he pointed out that it would cause political arguments if it had that power-

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext:
May I say to my hon. friend that when he says "power" he is

using the wrong word. I said the committee should not be instructed to bring in recommendations, because they might take their time in debating political policies. I never said the committee had not power.

maintopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext:
I will refer my right hon. friend to the page. I shall not quote his remarks, because the hon. gentleman who preceded me succeeded in speaking sufficiently long to deny to us any discussion at length of what he said here this evening. The Prime Minister's remarks will foe found at pages 749 and 750 of Hansard, and when this debate is adjourned and the next opportunity comes I shall quote them.
I was dealing with the series of events. There were by-elections and there were pilgrimages. My hon. friends opposite, who for four long years sat silent in regard to this problem, and who during the last two years never opened their mouths with regard to it, suddenly developed courage. My hon. friend the member for Waterloo North (Mr. Breithaupt) led this valiant band of six to the Prime Minister, according to press reports of the highest authority, and there and then the Prime Minister found himself in a position where he had to take the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) to task because the Minister of Finance had been faithful in carrying out government policy during the last several months.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext: May I say to my hon. friend that is absolute nonsense. I never took the Minister of Finance to task in my life, nor did he ever take me to task.

maintopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext:
My right hon.
friend speaks but the truth, because so often infallibility has been his belief in his own decisions. There is no doubt about the truth of what I was saying, and the press must have been prescient, because its prophecies indeed came true. Last Saturday, a week ago today, information passed along the corridors of this house to the effect that, as a result of this meeting, the six members had convinced the Prime Minister that all was not as well as he said it was, following the results of the byelections. I am going to read what he said then. There was no suggestion then that inflation was not being controlled. There was no suggestion then that high prices were prevailing in this country, because the Prime Minister said, and I quote from the press statement:
While inflation may be bad, and takes time to control, it should never be forgotten that
there is one thing worse than inflation and that is depression.

Report of Prices Committee
These are the words that indicate the change of mind between June 9 and June 19, one week ago today. The Prime Minister said:
The federal government, at the risk of its own immediate popularity, has so shaped its policies as to restrict further inflation in the present, and to lessen the possibilities of depression later on. This, too, is a course of action not too readily understood.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext: What did my hon. friend say after the by-election?

maintopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext: I was not in power. The Prime Minister was giving alibis.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext: Farther away from it than ever.

maintopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Well, of course,
again the interruption of my hon. friend to the left indicates the close relationship oetween these two parties in the house.

maintopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext:
What happened in
Saskatchewan?

maintopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext:
I listened to my hon. friends. I have not been dealing with my hon. friends to the left, but they find it necessary to interrupt.
Within ten days a report was handed to certain members of this committee on prices. I say that one week ago today certain members of this committee, the government members, had the eight recommendations or so in their possession. Who gave them the recommendations? Will the Prime Minister answer who gave them the recommendations? Was it he, or the members of the cabinet who gave them to that committee that was to find facts on evidence? On the 9th of June the Prime Minister said, all is well.
Tile federal government, at the risk of its own immediate popularity, has so shaped its policies as to restrict further inflation.
And a few days later a report is handed to the members of the committee with the attitude, according to the hon. member for Eglinton, You take it, and if amendments are suggested they will be voted down. That, Mr. Speaker, is the attitude that should be taken by any committee chairman, by any vice-chairman, or by anyone connected with the committee.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext: I am sure the hon. member will permit me to say that I was in the chair when the resolutions were discussed, and I am sure the hon. member for Eglinton and every other hon. member of the committee will recall that I made no such remark.

maintopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext: It was made repeatedly by the vice-chairman.

maintopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext: We are at least succeeding in getting a word from the hon. gentleman who has interrupted.

maintopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext: He can look after himself.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext: Go build a house.

maintopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext: Mortimer Snerd.

maintopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext:
I am not going to make any observation about that. Then, within a few days these recommendations are handed out. Again I ask the Prime Minister, who was it that one week ago today drafted or handed certain members of the committee, certain government members of the committee, the recommendations that it was desired the committee should give? Surely wTe have the right to hear from the Prime Minister. Surely this country had the right to hear from the Prime Minister today. What is the government going to do about it?
According to the press of a week ago, and again it was prescient, as soon as the recommendations come before the house-possibly the Minister of National Defence is not following this-

maintopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext: He lives in Montreal.

maintopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Has he anything to say about it? What is the attitude of the government? I ask, why have they not given the necessary moneys to the combines investigator, as provided in recommendation No. 2? Two years ago they said, "Put teeth in the law and we will prosecute Qombines and monopolies." Now they say it was lack of money.
What is the next one? Recommendation No. 3 reads:
That the government amend the regulations of the appropriate legislation, if that be found necessary, so that immediate specific action can be taken wherever the evidence discloses flagrant cases of profiteering at the consumer's expense.
What do they want that for? They have the powers already under the Combines Investigation Act. They have it already in the Wartime Prices and Trade Board Act. They say again, as a stall, that, if necessary, further change be made. What is the government going to do about this recommendation, because did the recommendations not originate with the government? What is the government going to do about this?
That the government consider the removal of import restrictions now in effect on certain fruits and vegetables.
Surely this country has had the right today to learn what the government will do on this
Report of Prices Committee

report, not next year, not next session, but before this session closes. Let us do something in this house in regard to prices, whether along the lines here suggested or along whatever lines may be necessary for the purpose.
Since it is eleven o'clock, I move the adjournment of the debate.
On motion of Mr. Diefenbaker the debate was adjourned.
